maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. DAVIES
PRIVILEGE-MR. DAVIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. Last
Friday evening, the seventeenth, while the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) was discussing the second reading of Bill No. 24, to amend the criminal code, he referred to the question of where the communist party was raising its funds, and during the course of his remarks 'the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) interjected a remark to the effect that some of its funds came from the Conservative party. Upon being pressed for the source of his information the hon. member for Wetaskiwin is reported by Hansard to have replied, at page 2229, "From the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Davies)." Mir. Speaker, I deny ever having had any conversation with the hon. member for Wetaskiwin or anybody else on such a subject. I deny ever having made such a statement to him or to anybody else. I further deny that there is any truth whatever in his statement as reported. As a matter of fact, I was in the house at the time and I happened to notice that the hon. member for Wetaskiwin used the word "Ask" the hon. member for Athabaska, not "From," and I would ask that a correction accordingly be made in Hansard.

subtopic: TRADE WITH UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: PROPOSED RECIPROCAL ARRANGEMENT FOR EXCHANGE OF NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the government of Canada reopen negotiations with the government of the United States of America with a view of bringing about a satisfactory reciprocal trade arrangement between Canada and the United States whereby the natural products of Canada, that is the products of the sea, the farm, the mines, and the forests, and including fish, lumber, wheat, cattle, etc., should have free entry into the United States in exchange for the admission of certain goods from the United States of America, which in the interests of both countries may be admitted into Canada, free from customs tariffs.
Trade with United States

He said: Mr. Speaker, in drafting the resolution which I have just moved I endeavoured to be as careful as possible in the wording so that the matter could be discussed entirely from a business point of view, and so that our discussion might centre around the question as to whether in the opinion of this house it is wise that this country should do all the business possible with our great neighbour to the south. In order that I may deal with this matter properly I should like, first, to give a history of the different negotiations between Canada and the United States with regard to what is commonly known as reciprocity. Or, in other words, I shall outline what might better be termed the different business relations which have existed at various time between those two great countries.
In 1854 a treaty known, as the Elgin-Marcy reciprocity treaty had been negotiated, and it proved beneficial to Canada, for the ten years the treaty was in operation.
The United States statesmen claimed, however, that it had not been so beneficial to that country, and therefore the radical Republicans in the United States Senate voted for its abrogation. One reason why the vote was so strong against it then, in the United States Senate, it is said, was that it was done in retaliation against the British attitude toward the south, during the Civil war.
In 1866, A. T. Galt, Minister of Finance, and W. P. Howland, Postmaster General in Canada, went to Washington, in an effort to secure to Canada a continuance of the benefits of free trade, and to propose that such trade be established by reciprocal legislation.
After confederation, when Sir John Macdonald was Prime Minister of this country, in an effort to hold both the Conservative and Liberal factions under his control, he favoured reciprocity with the United States, providing the provisions of the old treaty could be renewed.
In 1869, Sir John Rose, then Minister of Finance, went to Washington to confer with Secretary Fish of the United States government. There was much speculation as to what Rose had offered Fish as a basis for a renewal of the reciprocity treaty.
Sir John Rose assumed another important position, in the story of Canadian-American relations, when he went to Washington in 1871 to pave the way for a settlement of the troublesome Alabama claims dispute. Other methods had failed to settle the matter, and now the British government suggested that Rose offer the fisheries and the use of the St. Lawrence waterway, as a basis

for proceeding to the more serious points of disagreement.
A fisheries agreement, which favoured the United States, was to run for fifteen years, and the right to the use of the St. Lawrence was granted to the United States forever.
When the Mackenzie government was formed-about 1872-3-with Sir Richard Cartwright as Finance Minister, one of the first things the Liberal government did was to make a serious attempt to negotiate a reciprocity treaty with the United States.
A treaty was drafted which provided that the duties on the articles in three separate schedules should from July 1875 to July 1876 be two-thirds of the present duties, that they should be reduced to one-third the following year, and that after 1877 and for a period of twenty-one years, the articles on these three schedules were to enter each country free of duty. The first schedule contained a long list of natural products. The second contained forty articles some of which were manufactured articles; and the third a long list of manufactures.
Although the treaty was submitted to the Senate of the United States the proposal was rejected by that body.
In 1879, with the Macdonald government in power in Canada, the rates of duties on manufactured articles, were increased, although a reciprocity clause was attached to this tariff which fulfilled the election campaign promises. It provided that whenever the United States allowed Canadian natural products to enter the country free of duty, then Canada would allow the same articles to enter this country free of customs duties.
The Conservatives, from that time on, made reciprocity proposals upon the basis of this offer of 1879.
It was some years afterwards before another effort was made to secure a reciprocal arrangement. The fisheries dispute paved the way, in the next attempt, just as it had in certain previous ones. The Canadians had recognized the importance of the north Atlantic fisheries, as a lever to force concessions from the American authorities in the direction of freer trade.
The treaty of Washington of 1871 put an end to the fisheries dispute after fifteen years. The time approached for the agreement to come to an end and Canadians prepared to make the best of the opportunity.
Sir Charles Tupper went to Washington in 1888 and had a conference with Secretary of State Bayard. The Canadian offer was to give free fish for free trade in natural products. A treaty was arranged and sent to the United States Senate, but was not rati-

Trade with United States
fied. The "Commercial Union" movement is the most interesting phase of the long period of agitation for reciprocity between the two countries. It had its origin in Canada. Among the most active and enthusiastic leaders, however, were some Americans. Among the leaders were the following: Erastus Wiman, President of the Great Northwestern Telegraph Company, a Canadian by birth but residing in New Jersey; Goldwin Smith, eminent historian and scholar; Benjamin Butterworth, representative in congress from Cincinnati, Ohio; and Samuel J. Ritchie, an Akron, Ohio, manufacturer, owning nickel mines in Ontario. The latter and his legal adviser, Mr. Butterworth, spent much time and money in the spread of the doctrine.
The movement was first taken up by the Toronto Mail and later by the Toronto Globe. Commercial leagues were formed throughout the country. The doctrine actually involved an unrestricted trade with the pooling of customs duties, to be divided upon some agreed proportion.
In the spring of 1888 the leaders of the Liberal party in caucus decided, after some discussion, to support Sir Richard Cartwright in a motion for what he termed "Unrestricted Reciprocity" with the United States. Conservatives and Liberals alike had supported reciprocity and many Conservatives had supported the doctrine of "Commercial Union." It 'had not yet become a party issue. When Cartwright introduced his resolution it served as a challenge. When George E. Foster arose early in the debate and offered an amendment to the main motion which stated that the government would adhere to the standing offer of 1879 the issue was clear. It had become a party question. The debate originally intended for but two or three days, dragged on for a month. Cartwright and his followers had to distinguish between commercial union and unrestricted reciprocity. The Conservatives attacked the Liberal motion chiefly because it included discrimination against the mother country and would lead, they insisted, to political union. The motion was defeated by a party vote of 124 to 67. There were four New Brunswick Conservatives who voted for the motion.
In 1890 the Colonial Secretary of Newfoundland, the Hon. Robert Bond, went to Washington and succeeded in drawing up a convention with Mr. Blaine which provided for freer trade between the two countries. When Sir John A. Macdonald heard of this he sent Sir Charles Tupper to Washington, who suggested that they proceed to base a treaty on the Elgin treaty of 1854, as a
basis for a new agreement. But Mr. Blaine insisted that that treaty was not wide enough. Sir Charles Tupper returned to Canada and intimated that an arrangement could be made. Macdonald and Tupper were urged to go to the people, in a general election, if they could assure the electorate they were negotiating a reciprocal arrangement with the United States.
In 1892 Canadian commissioners led by Mr. (Foster again presented their case to the American government. Nothing further was done in the matter until 1911, when the Hon. W. S. Fielding and the Hon. William Paterson proceeded to Washington and negotiated a reciprocity treaty which was known as the Taft-Fielding proposal. This treaty was defeated in the general election of 1911.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is another matter which is closely allied with the reciprocity negotiations. In fact the reciprocity conversations and negotiations were really a result of the treaty of 1818 between the British government and the United States government, and in view of the present agitation regarding the renewal of the so-called modus vivendi, it would be as well to give also the history surrounding it. Article 1 of the treaty stipulated-
(a) That the inhabitants of the United States shall have forever in common with British subjects the "liberty" to take fish of every kind on a portion of the coast of Newfoundland, about the Magdialen islands, and on the north shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence eastward from Point Joli, and to dry and cure fish on the said portion of the north shore so long as it remained unsettled, and afterwards by agreement with the settlers.
(bl That the United States renounce forever the liberty claimed on the other parts of the coast for their fishermen, but that they would be permitted to enter bays and harbours on all portions of the Canadian coast for wood, water, shelter and repairs "but for no other purpose whatever."
The two countries placed different interpretations on certain parts of the above article of the treaty and difficulties arose. Consequently the Reciprocity treaty of 1854, mentioned previously, resulted, and fish and fish products of each country were admitted free of duty into the other and reciprocal fishing privileges were authorized in certain territorial waters of each country.
It was out of this treaty of 1888 that the system of issuing what are called modus vivendi licences to the United States fishing vessels was started. May I say here modus vivendi means a working arrangement, a practical compromise. The British plenipotentiaries feeling that it would take some time to have the treaty made effective recom-
Trade with United States

mended a modus vivendi not to last more than two years, under which United States fishing vessels, by the payment of a fee of one dollar and fifty cents per registered ton, could obtain the port privileges contemplated by the treaty and thus avoid the difficulties that would ensue while limiting such vessels to their liberties under the treaty of ISIS. The privileges were (a) the purchase of bait, ice, seines, lines, and all other supplies and outfits and the transhipment of catch and the shipping of crews.
These licences were yearly continued thereafter and in 1802 an act was passed giving the governor in council power to authorize the issue of the licences. This act formed section three of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act.
In 1918 on the recommendation of an International Fisheries Commission, the privileges covered by the modus vivendi were granted reciprocally in either country to the fishing vessels of the other.
In 1921 the United States gave notice that the privileges granted in 1918 were to be terminated in that country. They were continued, however, in Canada without licence until the season of 1922 when the modus vivendi licences were again introduced, but later in that year the fee for the licence was reduced from one dollar and fifty cents per ton to a nominal sum of one dollar per vessel. The authority of council was given for the granting of such licences at the nominal fee for that year and the following year.
As a result of some agitation on the Atlantic coast for the discontinuance of the modus vivendi privileges to United States fishing vessels unless the United States recognized the advantages of such privileges, it was decided by order in council of November, 1923, that modus vivendi licences should not be continued after the end of that year. The United States government was so notified, and from that date until the present time no modus vivendi licences have been issued and United States vessels are now restricted to the simple privileges of entering our bays and harbours for the purpose of obtaining wood, water, shelter and repairs but for no other purpose whatsoever.
As I said a moment ago, in dealing with this question, which to my mind is a very serious one, especially as far as the maritime provinces are concerned, I intend only to deal with the question of the fisheries. Before dealing with what I consider would be the benefits of reciprocity may I speak for a moment in regard to what is known as the modus vivendi? From this history which I have given it appears clearly that during the
[Mr. Duff.)
years the modus vivendi was in operation United States fishing vessels could come into our ports and buy bait and supplies and tranship fish. There was a good deal of business done in the maritime provinces. I have always been a great advocate of freedom of trade. I am trying to keep as far away as I can from the political side of this matter, but I never could see why under the treaty of ISIS or subsequent treaties the late Liberal government or previous governments in this country would not allow United States fishing vessels to come into Canadian ports and do business with us. I notice, in reading the newspapers the last few months, that my good friend the member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) was in Ottawa and strongly recommended to the government that the modus vivendi arrangement should be reopened so that fishing vessels could come into Canadian ports. I want to thank him for the great interest he has taken in the matter. I am only sorry that the newspaper reported that his idea was that every year these privileges should be granted only for the space of three months. I intend to prove that if it is a good thing that American fishing vessels be allow'ed to come into our ports for bait, ice, provisions and supplies for three months it would be a much better thing if they were allowed to come in for the whole year. I notice that in the Halifax Herald of Saturday a dispatch from Ottawa headed:
Privileges are Being Restored to United States Schooners
And the dispatch goes on to say:
The privileges, it is stated, are to be restored for a limited period, believed to be six weeks, particularly to provide for the sale of bait of which there is a large supply in Nova Scotia cold storage plants.
I hope that dispatch is only partly true. Again I say I am strongly in favour of opening our ports to United States fishing vessels; not for six weeks or three months, but for as many years as those vessels want to do business with us.

speechtext:
I intend to deal with that question in a moment. It will be noticed, Mr. Speaker, that this dispatch says that the reason for granting these United States vessels the privilege of coming into our ports for six weeks is that certain cold storage plants have a large supply of bait. If these vessels had been allowed to come into our ports for

Trade with United States
twelve months of the year these cold storage plants would not have had this large quantity of bait on hand. I am very much afraid that if this arrangement is made for six weeks it will only give the cold storage plants a chance to get rid of their bait, with the result that the same thing will happen again that has happened in previous years.
If the United States fishing vessels can enter our ports twelve months of the year they can buy bait direct from the fishermen; if they are allowed to enter only for six weeks they will have to buy bait at the cold storage plants. This means that the plants-the big interests, if you like to call them that-who buy bait from the fishermen at ridiculously low prices and put it in their cold storage plants, will sell that same bait to the United States fishermen at higher prices. Last year I knew of traps full of herring and squid that had to be opened so that the herring and squid could escape because there was no one to buy them. If United States fishing vessels had been allowed to buy bait then probably these fishermen could have sold their catches. I know of another case not a thousand miles from my own home. There was no demand for bait; the squid, the best bait that can be bought, were sold by the fishermen to the cold storage plants for 30 cents a bushel, and herring was sold to the same plants for 25 cents a bushel. If United States fishermen had been allowed to come to Nova Scotia ports and buy that bait direct from the fishermen, instead of the poor devil of a fisherman getting 30 cents a bushel for bait which was later sold by the cold storage plants for 4 cents a pound, he would have received SI or $1.50 a bushel. I commend the government for considering the opening of Nova Scotia ports, but if they are going to open them at all they should be kept open so that the fishermen along the shores of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick will be able to sell their bait direct to United States and Canadian fishing vessels, which will give them a better return.
I said I was in favour of these vessels coming to our ports, not only to buy bait
but to buy ice as well. This would mean that the ice houses in Canso, Lunenburg, Yarmouth and other places would be filled with ice which would be sold to the fishermen. Then my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) asked me a question. Certainly I am in favour of allowing United States vessels to trans-ship their catches in bond from Nova Scotia ports to Boston. Of course we are all interested in the fishermen and in our fisheries, but I think it will be admitted-and I say this with all modesty- that I am just as much interested in the fishermen of Nova Scotia as anyone else, and I say that if we allow United States vessels to come to Canadian ports and trans-ship their fish it will mean more labour for Canadian workmen. Ice will have to be bought. Boxes will have to be made from Canadian lumber by Canadian workmen. Men will have to pack the fish in the boxes; teamsters will have to haul the fish to the railway station; the Canadian National railways will get the haul to Yarmouth, and the steamer will carry the fish to Boston, New York or wherever they go. Surely there can be no harm in that. It will not hurt Canadian fishermen if we allow this practice to be carried on. These fish do not come in competition with fish caught by Canadian fishermen; they go direct to United States ports. So I will say that I am strongly in favour of allowing these vessels to enter our ports throughout the year so that they can do business with us and spend their good American money here.
I said that I intended to deal with only one phase of this subject, Mr. Speaker, but it might be interesting if I were to place on Hansard a statement showing the exports of certain qualities of fish shipped from Canada during the years 1919, 1926 and 1931. This statement shows our total exports of certain kinds of fish to British Empire countries and to the United States, including Puerto Rico. I have not time to read the whole statement, but I am going to ask that it be placed on Hansard so that hon. members may have the benefit of these figures.

speechtext:
My hon. friend asks who imposed the duty; the United States, of course. Now, in my opinion, with the Canadian fisheries in their present condition, there is only one salvation for them and that is for this government to make a trade arrangement
with the United States so that our fish might go into that country.
We hear a good deal about trawlers nowadays. I have no time to go into that question to-day, but if we had the United States for a market there would not be very much talk about trawlers because the trouble to-day is that Canada is a very small market. Great Britain is too far away from us, being some twenty-five hundred miles across the water, and they have their own source of supply so far as fish is concerned, so that practically the only market open to us now, to which we can extend our business, is the United States. I need not say that the fisheries of this country are in a deplorable condition, and I appeal to the government to do everything they can to help the industry. There is no question about it that there is a great opportunity for the government as well as for the fishermen of Canada. We read over the lintel at the main entrance to this building these words:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
What is the use of having the wholesome sea at both our gates if we do not take advantage of it? The sea is full of fish and our fishermen are only too ready to catch them if they could get a half decent market, but when they have to face a duty of hundreds of thousands of dollars there is no hope for them. I do not blame this country, but the fact is that there is a duty which the United States government has imposed which makes it impossible for the fishermen of this country to carry on their operations in a proper manner. I think the time is ripe for something to be done if we are to be clear of our surplus product. This is the time for the government to enter into negotiations with the government of the United States.
In January I noticed in the Cosmopolitan magazine an interview given by Presidentelect Roosevelt, in which he made this statement:
This plan must go into effect at the same time that international trade is being restored through tariff adjustments. Every major problem before us to-day is involved with the tariff. The building of a higher tariff fence about ourselves has caused foreign retaliatory tariffs and prevented even the simple exchange and barter of goods internationally. By reciprocal agreements with other nations we shall have opportunity given to lower our tariff fence to permit the resumption of international trade. The United States can lead in outlining the mutual restoration of trade, and thus facilitate exchange.
Those are the words of President-elect Roosevelt and, I repeat, the time is ripe for this government to do something in the matter. Let me give some quotations from
22G0
Trade with United States

prominent authorities. Sir Robert Borden, Canadian 'head of Barclay's bank, declares that:
The removal of restrictions that impede the interchange of products is the crying need of nations suffering from the depression.
Certainly the fishermen of this country are suffering not only from the present depression but from restricted markets, and neither this nor any other government could do anything better than to endeavour to obtain a market for the Canadian fishermen.
Sir Herbert Holt, in his annual report of the Royal Bank of Canada, deplored:
. . . the futility of the trade warfare of which tariffs are the most important weapon.
Sir John Aird, president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce wants:
... a general and uniform reduction of tariffs the world over.
Mr. S. J. Moore of the Bank of Nova Scotia:
. . . sees the nations in a state of economic siege, trying to starve one another out of an impossible position.
And Mr. J. A. McLeod, of the Bank of Nova Scotia, calls for:
. . . sweeping reciprocal reductions in tariffs among all countries.
Surely Mr. McLeod's words, if they mean anything, are to be taken as including the United States in the desire for sweeping reciprocal reductions. We have heard a good deal about Mr. Roger Babson. As quoted in the Halifax Herald, New Year's issue, this gentleman makes the following statement:
Existing tariff discriminations whereby Nova Scotia is unable to sell her fish, coal and lumber and other products to the Atlantic seaboard territories which constitute your natural markets; and yet is compelled to pay from 25 per cent to 50 per cent additional on automobiles, clothing, shoes and practically all manufactured goods. The maritime provinces should have a separate tariff with the United States.
I do not agree with that last statement, because I think we should have only one tariff in the country; but there is no reason why a proper arrangement could not be made with our great neighbour to the south, so far as Nova Scotia and the maritimes are concerned.
Captain O'Donnell of the Eastern Steamships Company, in the same paper makes this statement:
In order that you may trade with the United States and she in turn shall offer you what she produces we must in some way bring about tariff adjustments that will be to the advantage

of all of us who live on each side of the line dividing our countries-the line on which there is not a single fortress or a suggestion that we are not neighbours and friends who trust each other.
I have here another statement giving the views of the premier of Nova Scotia, as published in the same issue of the Halifax Herald to which I have referred:
Our lumbering and fishing industries in so far as they rely upon export markets have experienced the difficulties consequent upon the lack of purchasing power in their former markets and this situation has been aggravated by adverse tariffs and unfavourable exchange.
In view of all these expressions of opinion, I think I am justified in asking the government, at the earliest opportunity, to approach the great country to the south of us, a country which has a potential market for Canada of 120,000,000 people, with a view to securing an outlet for our fish products. I am sure that with the experience which they have gone through in the last five or six years, the United States must realize that the duties they have placed on fish, both in the Fordney-McCumber and in the Hawley-Smoot tariffs, have not helped the fishermen of the United States, while they have been detrimental to those of Canada.
I hope that the suggestion will not be made either in this debate or in the country, but it might be said that if we entered into a reciprocal trade arrangement or a commercial arrangement with the United States there would be danger of this country being too closely connected with our southern neighbour. I do not think for a moment that the people of Canada will sell their birthright for a mess of pottage. We. are loyal citizens of the British Empire. If we sell our fish, lumber or anything else to the greatest, the nearest and the most natural market, as far as the maritime provinces are concerned, then I say we should fear no danger. We are daughters in our mother's house and mistress in our own. We are going to remain daughters in our mother's house and all we ask of the British Empire, all we ask of this country is to stand by the maritime provinces and give us a reciprocal trade arrangement with the United States so that we can do business with and make money in dealing in a businesslike and reciprocal manner with them.

speechtext:
We shall deal with that
presently.
In view of the present condition of economic matters in the world, I think it well to make a more extended statement than I otherwise would with respect to this particular matter. It is well to remember the historic background in connection with reciprocity and it is also well to remember that the remedy which the hon. gentleman seeks is one that is not in our hands to grant. If we keep these two facts in mind I think perhaps we will be able to approach this problem without prejudice and without any feeling of resentment against another country that has pursued a fiscal policy which to its representatives in congress seems best. This is just as we have done. If we concede the right to others to do that which we ourselves have done, we will then probably be able to appreciate the problem more clearly than if we claimed the right, on the one hand, to do as we pleased and, on the other, denied that right to others.
In 1879 when the national policy was introduced in this country, section 6 of the legislation provided as follows:
6.	Any or all of the following articles,- that is to say: animals of all kinds, green fruit, hay. straw, bran, seeds of all kinds, vegetables (including potatoes and other roots), plants, trees, and shrubs, coal and coke, salt, hops, wheat, peas and beans, barley, rye, oats, Indian corn, buckwheat and all other grain, flour of wheat and flour of rye, Indian meal and oatmeal, and flour or meal of any other grain, butter, cheese, fish (salted or smoked), lard, tallow, meats (fresh, salted or smoked), and lumber, may be imported into Canada free of duty, or at a less rate of duty than is provided by this act, upon proclamation of the governor in council, which may be issued whenever it appears to his satisfaction that similar articles from Canada may be imported into the United States free of duty, or at a rate of duty not exceeding that payable on the same under such proclamation when imported into Canada.
In introducing his budget upon that occasion the late Sir Leonard Tilley made an observation which I think it might be well for me to read. He said:
I have this to say to our American friends: Is 1865 they abrogated the reciprocity treaty,
and from that day to the present a large portion of the imports from that country into the dominion have been admitted free. We have hoped, but hoped in vain, that by the adoption of that policy we w-ould lead our American friends to treat us in a more liberal spirit with regard to the same articles. Well, after having waited twelve years for the consideration of this subject, the government requiring more revenue, have determined to ask this house to impose upon the products of the United States that have been free, such a duty as may seem consistent with our position. But the government couple with the proposal, in order to show that we approach this question with no unfriendly spirit, a resolution that will be laid on the table containing a proposition to this effect: That, as to articles named, which are the natural products of the country, including lumber, if the United States take off the duties in part or in whole, we are prepared to meet them with equal concessions. The government believe in a reciprocity tariff, yet may discuss free trade or protection, but the question of to-day is-Shall we have a reciprocity tariff, or a one-sided tariff?
That was in 1879. That legislation remained upon the statute books of this country in that or some modified form for very many years. In fact, that section, the terms of which I have just read, section 6 in the legislation of 1879, will be found in the revised statutes of 1886. In 1888 there was a revision of the proposals, but in the main they remained as I have read them. The legislation of 1888 was somewhat different from 'that of 1879, and in order that there may 'be no misapprehension on the part of the house as to what the proposals of this parliament have been-when I say this parliament, I mean that although the proposals were introduced by the government of the day in the end they were crystallized into legislation which constituted the offer which the parliament of Canada made to our great neighbour with respect to the matters to which I refer-I shall read section 9 of the legislation of 1888, which is slightly different from the section I read first. The words are as follows:
9.	Any or all of the following things, that is to say: Animals of all kinds, hay, straw, vegetables (including potatoes and other roots), salt, peas, beans, barley, malt, rye, oats, buckwheat, flour or rye, oatmeal, buckwheat flour, butter, cheese, fish of all kinds, fish oil, products of fish and of all other creatures living in the water, fresh meats, poultry, stone or marble in its crude or unwrought state, lime, gypsum or plaster of paris (ground, unground, or calcined), hewn or wrought or unwrought burr and grindstones, and timber and lumber of all kinds unmanufactured in whole or in part, including shingles, clapboards, and w-ood pulp, may be imported into Canada free of duty, or at less rate of duty than is provided for by an act at the time in force, upon proclamation of the Governor General, which may be issued whenever it appears to his satisfaction that similar
Trade with United States

articles from Canada may be imported into the United States free of duty, or at a rate of duty not exceeding that payable on the same under such proclamation when imported into Canada.
It will be observed that this list contains items which were not in the first list, and that the first list contains items deleted from this one. In 1800 there was a reenactment of the terms of section 9 of 1888. In 1894, fifteen years after the original offer had been made in 1879, there was a substantial modification in the terms of the proposals. Section 7, 8, 10, 11, 12 and 24 of chapter 33 of the statutes of that year contain the offer or proposals of the dominion parliament in that regard. Sections 7, 8 and 10 read:
7.	The whole or part of the duties hereby imposed upon fish and other products of the fisheries may be remitted as respects either the United States or Newfoundland, or both, upon proclamation of the governor in council, which may be issued whenever it appears to his satisfaction that the governments of the United States and Newfoundland, or of either of them, have made changes in their tariffs of duties imposed upon articles imported from Canada, in reduction or repeal of the duties in force in the said countries respectively.
8.	Eggs may be imported into Canada free of duty, or at a less duty than is provided for by this act, upon proclamation of the governor in council, which may be issued whenever it appears to his satisfaction that eggs from Canada may be imported into the United States free of duty, or at a rate of duty not exceeding that payable on eggs under such proclamation when imported into Canada.
10.	Shingles and pulp wood, or either of them, may be imported into Canada free of duty, upon proclamation of the governor in council, which may be issued whenever it appears to his satisfaction that shingles and pulp wood, or either of them, from Canada may be imported into the United States free of duty.
Then section 11 reads:
Any or all of the following things, that is to say: green or ripe apples, beans, buckwheat, pease, potatoes, rye, rye-flour, hay, and vegetables specified in item 41 in schedule A to this act, shall be free of duty when imported into Canada from the country of production, upon proclamation of the governor in council, which may be issued whenever it appears to his satisfaction that such country imposes no duty on the like product or products imported into it from Canada.
It will be observed that instead of limiting the proposed offer to the United States of America, it is extended to any country which grants reciprocal benefits to this country.
Then barley and Indian corn were dealt with by section 12:
Barley and Indian corn shall be free of duty when imported into Canada from the country of production, upon proclamation of the governor in council, which may be issued whenever it appears to his satisfaction that such country whence either or both these products are imported admits both these products free of duty imported into it from Canada.

By this statute the acts that I have just previously quoted were repealed. That contains the offers that were made up to that day, and it might be well in this regard to refer to the speech that was made by the late Right Hon. George E. Foster on March 27, 1890, when this and the similar section that I have just read were under consideration :
I now come to another item about which there has been considerable discussion in the house, and out of it. It is that which relates to plants, fruits, shrubs and the like, and with which this house dealt in 1888. By an order in council of April 14, 1888, certain fruits and plants and shrubs were placed upon the free list. This arose from the fact that in the Tariff Act of 1879, there was a clause which left it permissive with the government, on a certain list of articles, to either reduce the duty upon them or to remove the duty altogether when such articles were either free, or of less duty in the United States than was charged here. The matter was brought to the attention of the government in 1888 under the peculiar circumstances which at that time prevailed. It was contended by gentlemen of the opposition that it was not treating the United States fairly, when they had any one of these articles at a lower duty, if we did not place that article on the same tariff footing as it was in the United States. It was contended on this side of the house that this clause of the act was simply permissive and not mandatory on the government and that it rested with the government of Canada to say whether this should be done in individual instances or not. and that what was contemplated in that article in the tariff law was that when those products as a whole, or as many of them as Canada should consider it to be in her interest to reciprocate in, were placed on the free list or had a lower rate of duty imposed upon them, the government would reduce its duties upon them, to the same level. However, under the circumstances that prevailed at that time, it was decided to put these articles on the free list, and a very considerable amount of duty was lost in consequence, and a very considerable damage was done to a large and important interest in this country.
I read that merely to indicate that at that time there was a contention made that the offer must be taken as a whole, rather than that the individual items that constituted the offer Should be considered if the circumstances warranted. In the event, it transpired that the government of the day treated the offer as referring to individual items. In 1891, the year following the speech to which I have just referred, the finance minister, still the Right Hon. George E. Foster, said:
But I may say this, that the government holds itself ready, as the Liberal-Conservative governments have always done, to meet the United States on a fair and equitable basis and with the sincere and earnest desire to remove all differences that exist and to give the greatest freedom of trade compatible with the best interests of this country in its relations with the United States of America. Certainly no govern-

Trade with United States
ment of a self-governing and self-respecting country should be asked to do more. Further than this, we can state that while wre are willing to make all the concessions that on these lines can fairly be made, we are not willing to go so far as to injuriously 6hut ourselves out from the trade which we have with Great Britain and the other countries in the world, that we are not willing to forego, for a doubtful gain, the substantial advantages which we have enjoyed and expect to enjoy from our relations with the mother country, from which connection we have reaped so much in the past and from which we hope so much in the future.
Then in the speech of 1894, in which a revision of the offer was made, as I have just read, these words were used by the Right Hon. George E. Foster:
When we come to the grains-oats have been kept at 10 cents per bushel, and cornmeal at 40 cents per barrel, but two schedules have been formed with other grains, and two or three other agricultural products, The first schedule contains corn and barley. The duties on these are kept -as they were before, but there is added this clause, "Provided that barley and Indian corn shall be free of duty when imported into Canada from the country of production, if such country, whence either or both are imported, admits both these products free of duty, when imported thence from Canada. That is an offer of reciprocity to any country that chooses to take it up.
The object of leaving oats out of that proposal was to retain protection to that product of the farmer in Canada, a very large product and one which, in some portions of Canada, might be adversely affected at certain times and under certain conditions, if the duty were removed. Then again buckwheat, buckwhat meal, rye, rye flour, beans, peas, hay, potatoes, green and ripe apples,' and vegetables, are left with the same duties, or nearly the same, as they had under the old tariff, and it is enacted that each of the above products shall be admitted free of duty from any country which imposes no duty on the like product when imported from Canada.
I repeat that by 1894 the parliament of Canada had extended the offer made in 1879 with respect to the countries that might accept it, because in 1894 the offer became open to all the countries of the world, whereas in 1879 it had reference only to the United States, and later to Newfoundland. So that the effect between 1879 and 1894 was to induce the Canadian people, speaking through their representatives in this parliament, to place upon the statute books an offer that was open to all the world with respect to the items to which I have referred. After the change of administration in 1896 it will be recalled that certain reciprocal offers were made, and I think perhaps it might be advantageous to refer to them.
Section 7 of chapter 16 of the revised statutes of 1897 reads as follows:
The whole or part of the duties hereby imposed upon fish and other products of the
fisheries may be remitted as respects either the United States or Newfoundland, or both, upon proclamation of the governor in council, which may be issued, whenever it appears to his satisfaction that the governments of the United States and Newfoundland, or either of them, have made changes in their tariffs of duties imposed upon articles imported from Canada, in reduction or repeal of the duties in force in the said countries respectively.
Then there was a protective clause with respect to the French treaty of 1894. Section 16 reads:
Nothing contained in the foregoing provisions shall affect the French Treaty Act, 1894, or chapter three of the statutes of 1895, intituled An Act respecting Commercial Treaties affecting Canada.
Then follows section 17:
17. When the customs tariff of any country admits the products of Canada on terms which, on the whole, are as favourable to Canada as the terms of the reciprocal tariff herein referred to are to the countries to which it may apply, articles which are the growth, produce, or manufacture of such country, when imported direct therefrom, may then be entered for duty, or taken out of warehouse for consumption in Canada, at the reduced rates of duty, provided in the reciprocal tariff set forth in schedule D to this act.
2.	Any question arising as to the countries entitled to the benefits of the reciprocal tariff shall be decided by the controller of customs, subject to the authority of the governor in council.
3.	The governor in council may extend the benefits of the reciprocal tariff to any country entitled thereto by virtue of a treaty with Her Majesty.
4.	The controller of customs may make such regulations as are necessary for carrying out the intention of this section.
The house will observe that instead of declaring that the benefits might be clearly reciprocal, the words used were "on the whole." That is, if on consideration of the whole tariff proposals it was clear that the benefits this country would derive would equal the benefits this country was offering or giving or granting, then the reciprocal arrangement would apply by virtue of the proclamation. That, too, was an extension of the general principle that began in 1879. That is, we find in 1897 not any astute desire to find equality through the crossing of a "t" or the dotting of an "i", but rather, if on the whole the benefits were at least equal, the reciprocal provisions should obtain.
Then we have further a consideration of this matter by reason of the fact that there was a continuous increase in the American tariff. The McKinley tariff had been increasing the then tariff of the United States, the Dingley tariff and the tariffs that followed, until the advent into power of the Democratic administration under President
Trade with United States

Wilson, when there was a complete revision of the tariffs and a reduction resulting in free entry into the United States markets of many of our commodities. This was coupled with a reciprocal provision in the American Tariff Act whereby on proclamation they could admit into their markets free certain commodities produced in Canada, if Canada took similar action. It will be remembered that pursuant to that provision the Dominion of Canada did issue a proclamation whereby wheat, flour and semolina were given free entry into the Canadian market, and as a result we had free entry into the American market.
The matter of course engaged the attention of the new administration of 1896. Perhaps it will be within the memory of most hon. members in this house that the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier set up a commission which went to Washington for the purpose of ascertaining just what could be done to extend our trade in that direction. It will also be recalled that in the end that mission failed. We find that in 1910 the late Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, in his budget speech used these words:
Wre had had negotiations from time to time with our American friends in relation to better trade conditions, and they had not turned out very successfully. We had, after repeated efforts, taken the ground that we should not again approach the United States with proposals for betterment of our trade relations, and that, if the matter was to be reopened again, it should be reopened, not upon the initiative of Canada, but upon the initiative of the United States. Accordingly, we declined to make any approach to the United States while the question of the French treaty was pending.
We claimed that our treaty with France was a treaty of reciprocity; that is to say, that we granted to France certain concessions in return for which France granted us similar or equivalent concessions. We said to the United States; If you want these concessions that France received from us, you should be prepared to purchase them as France did by giving what we would regard as equivalent concessions. To that our friends in the United States naturally demurred. They claimed that if they gave us what is called the favoured nation treatment- the best that was going-that we should do the same with them. That, however, was a view we ought not to take. We refused to take it in the beginning, and we refuse to take it now.
Those were the words of Mr. Fielding in 1910 after, as you will remember, an earnest effort had been made by the Canadian government of that day to induce our American friends to enter into a trade agreement.
In 1911, the next year, an agreement was entered into which was not quite what the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat described. It was not a treaty; the hon. member referred to it as such. On more than one 
occasion I have in this house indicated clearly the reasons I for one was opposed to that measure. First, it was an agreement incorporated into the statutes of both countries for that year, and it mentioned a limited number of items. But it was so framed that the change by this dominion of its tariff with respect to any one of those items terminated the agreement; secondly, the agreement was for no period of time, or for no definite length of years. It merely meant that if the interests of the United States could best be served by terminating it, all they had to do was to change the tariff rate on any single item, and the agreement then fell by the way. Equally, if the Dominion of Canada came to a similar conclusion and changed a single item, then, the agreement fell. I have made this statement so frequently that I hesitate to trouble the house to listen again, but I shall repeat that in my judgment any trade agreement which creates a channel of trade that may be terminated at the caprice or without notice to the other party, or be terminated by one party without considering the interests of the other, is fatal to the interests of both, because there is always a conflict of interest. All the terms of the agreement no longer have any appplication if, by reason of changed conditions one of the parties concludes the best thing it can do is to terminate the agreement by merely changing the tariff in regard to one item.
The people of Canada rejected the proposal, and I believe if they were asked again they would conclude that any arrangement which left us in a position whereby our trade relations could be changed over night for any reason, good or bad, which might occur to the minds of the American congress, would not be a sound or sane venture for a country such as ours. That is, we cannot hope to develop the resources of our country or give it favourable position in the trade of the world if we render it possible for a channel of trade to be dammed up, shut off, diverted or ruined by any action which may be taken by another party without notice to or regard for ourselves. Whatever else may be said, the fact is that with the coming of the great war the agreement could not have remained in the terms in which it stood because it would have been essential for either one or both of the parties to have modified it.
In the meantime, as will be remembered the Democratic party having come into power, and President Wilson's policy being that of lower tariffs, we had access to the American market for our wheat, cattle and many other commodities under terms which were highly satisfactory to Canadian producers.

Trade with United States
There then came a change of administration in the United States and also a change of administration in Canada. The Liberal party was in power in this country and the Republican party in power in the United States. The old veteran Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding, was again in his former position. I think it is fair to say that everything reasonable men could do compatible with self respect and regard for the honour of their country was done by the Minister of Finance of that day to secure lower tariffs from the United States. But the efforts failed.
I find that in 1923, after the new Republican administration was in power, Mr. Fielding in his budget speech used these words:
In the name of the Liberal party of Canada, I declare to-day that we stand for reciprocity with the United States. I say that when the opportunity comes to make a fair treaty or agreement-and I say the agreement of 1911 was a fair and reasonable agreement and I am glad that our Progressive friends call for a repetition of that agreement in their motion to-day; to that extent I agree with it-but I say that when the opportunity comes we are proud to declare in the face of the parliament of Canada, whatever the fate of it may be, that this Liberal party stands for reciprocity with the United States when we can get a fair and reasonable agreement. That is our position. We are content to let the people judge between the hon. gentleman and ourselves on that point.
And towards the close of the debate, on May 23, 1923, the right hon. gentleman opposite who is now leader of the opposition used these words:
What is the position with regard to the United States? Since the Liberal convention was held, there lias been enacted by the United States a much higher tariff than ever before existed between Canada and the United States. The Fordney-McCumber tariff, so-called, to-day is operating to the disadvantage of Canada. Is there any member of this house who will stand up in his place and say: Nothwithstanding that obvious fact we think we should throw down our bars against the United States and give them an opportunity to come in here and affect our industries in a manner even more seriously than they have already been affected.
Now, sir, I conceive those words to be words to which I can give my hearty support. I have said on more than one occasion, when the right hon. gentleman was leader of the government, that those words express, I believe, the general view of the Canadian people.
Is there any member of this house who will stand up in his place and say: Notwithstanding that obvious fact we think we should throw down our bars against the United States and give them an opportunity to come in here and affect our industries in a manner even more seriously than they have already been affected.
That was in 1923, it indicated the view which I believe was a reflection of the sound 53719-143
opinion of the Canadian people. And the right hon. gentleman proceeded in these words:
But, sir, we had another aim, and I think it is becoming apparent to anyone who reads the American press of to-day. The Americans, as I have said, have put up a high tariff wall against us affecting no part of this country more than the part from which my hon. friends the Progressive group come. They have that wall, but we want to show them that if they wish to sell they must also be ready to buy. There can be no jug-handled proposition in matters of trade. If you wish to sell you have got to be trilling to buy. If you wish to buy you have to be willing to sell. I think our American friends will come to see that if, as a result of their-and it is their own business, of course-if as a result of their action Canada is going to seek and obtain new markets in winch to buy and sell in Britain, new markets m France and new markets in Italy, is going to develop a reciprocal trade and eifect agreements with Australia and possibly other countries as well, if they begin to see that in all these directions we are striking out into and creating new lines of commerce, and that we can manage very well as we are, I am inclined to think that that line of thought, quicker than anything else, will bring about the change which my hon. friends of the Progressive group opposite hope may come.
I should think that is not an unsound argument. In this house on a previous occasion I made that statement, I now repeat it. May I in that regard point out that at that same session, dealing with the tariff, Mr. Fielding in his budget proposed what was enacted in the Revised Statutes of Canada, vol. 2, chapter 44, which was originally found in the statutes of 1923, chapter 42:
11.	If the President of the United States, under authority of the United States Tariff Act ot 1922. determines to reduce the duties imposed by such act on the following articles, that is to say:-
Cattle; wheat; wheat flour; oats; barley; potatoes; onions; turnips; hay; fish as enumerated in paragraphs 717. 718, 719, and 720 of the said Tariff Act of 1922,
The governor in council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on such articles imported into Canada from the United States as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for such reductions on Canadian products imported into the United States.
That was in 1923. That was the offer of the Liberal government of that day-not of the Liberal government, the offer of the parliament of Canada of that day, under which, as I have indicated, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance made the observations to which I have alluded. In face of that, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), instead of taking advantage of the offer as made and of the suggestion contained in the speeches of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, the tariff of the

Trade with United States

United States was raised against Canada higher still.
Now we are confronted with new conditions. I suggest to the hon. gentleman that he is asking this government to take a step which he should not ask it to take at this moment. If he earnestly desires to accomplish the purpose he has in mind-and he does-then obviously nothing should be done that would in any sense have the effect of lessening the possibility of success in the adoption of the arguments to which I have just referred, which are not my own but which I adopt, in dealing with the United States. If the hon. gentleman is prepared, as he apparently is, to accept the statements made in the interview by the president-elect, that is that by reciprocal agreements he proposes, nay he expects, to advance the trading interests of the United States, obviously any action taken by this parliament at this moment along the line suggested by the hon. gentleman would be premature. If we have the opportunity indicated in the statement made in the Cosmopolitan magazine and the interview to which the hon. gentleman referred of reliance by the new administration upon reciprocal agreements, then with our standing proposals, which have been the policy of all governments in this country since 1879 until to-day, it occurs to me that the hon. gentleman will best serve the interests that he desires to promote, having made the speech he has, and after such debate as may be thought desirable, by withdrawing the motion, in order that it may be made apparent to all who run and read that this parliament is still of the same opinion that it was in 1879, and that successive administrations have but given effect to one general view; that is that there is an earnest desire on the part of the Canadian people, with their great natural resources, their fisheries and forests and wide plains, to take advantage of the markets afforded by the most populous community in the world living together under one form of government.
But there is another reason, and I put it to the house as being, I submit, a conclusive reason why at this time, after this discussion, which cannot but be helpful, we should not adopt any resolution that would involve the possibility of being taken as an indication of a division of opinion. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the other day directed attention to the fact that a draft annotated agenda for the monetary and economic conference had been issued. I indicated that while that is a draft agenda only, it is now published, and any

person who so desired might avail himself of the opportunity to read it. Among the items on that agenda for consideration you will perhaps recall that after some difficulty this was added:
5.	Tariff and treaty policy.
A. Tariff policy:
(]) Cessation of tariff increases.
(2)	Reduction of tariffs.
(3)	Special aspects of the tariff problem.
(4)	Method of procedure.
I will not weary the house by reading from the annotations with respect to the item on the agenda, I will content myself by directing attention to the fact that the United States, with some reluctance, shall I say, has agreed to have placed on the agenda an item dealing with the question of tariffs.
Now every thoughtful Canadian realizes that our geographical position has imposed on us difficulties of the first order. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough in very mild and moderate terms referred to the preconfederation trading arrangements with the United States of America. Any man born as I was in the maritime provinces knows just what those trading agreements meant to the maritimes. There was then no Dominion of Canada, there was then no confederation. Reciprocal trading relations between the maritime provinces-not as a unit, of course, but each dealing with its own peculiar problems -and the United States of America gave a very substantial measure of prosperity to that part of this country. The termination of the treaty undoubtedly wrought great injury to the maritime provinces. But under the terms of the treaty it could be terminated, and the notice given was in accordance with the provisions of the treaty. It is undoubtedly true that where there was no treaty, as during the Wilson administration, the termination of that tariff arrangement by the legislative action of congress under the Republican administration did very great injury to the Dominion of Canada. There is no doubt that when channels of trade have been established, the destruction of such channels of trade, whether after six months' notice or without notice at all, works a very great injury on those who have created those channels. Our geographical position imposes upon this country extraordinary difficulties. No hon. member of this house who has had cause to think upon the problems of trade, as all have, fails to realize the truth of the statement by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) as to our natural market, if you can use that term when dealing with a foreign country, being the United States of America. I wonder how many members of

Trade with United States
this house have taken the trouble to study tihe situation according to the map: Look at the New England states and the city of New York, and remember the fast services by water, with splendid ships, that now exist between Yarmouth, we will say, and the city of New York. Think of the opportunities of modern cold storage facilities to supply the markets of that great city, whose population is at least half that of this dominion, with fish products just as fresh as could possibly be secured in any pant of the world.
On the other hand we have this argument, which 'has prevailed in the United States congress to this day: The Gloucester fishermen, and those of the New England towns, say that these hardy Newfoundlanders and mari-timers create unfair competition because of the quality of their products, which need not be here described, and they say they find it necessary to impose a duty of 2 cents a pound upon the fish brought to United States ports, as against free entry for fish caught by citizens of the United States. In dealing with a commodity such as fish, where the price per pound is not large, of course the result is that a 2 cent rate becomes such an addition to the cost as to represent practically a prohibition against the importation of Canadian fish. That is one item; I might mention others, but I will not take time to do so. These possibilities exist by reason of our geographical position and the easy transportation by water between the maritimes and the great cities and teeming communities of the eastern United States.
We must concede the absolute right of the United States congress to determine what it conceives to be best in the interests of that country. That is clear. In my judgment all we can do is follow the course that has been followed by successive governments and indicate clearly our willingness to negotiate on terms that are fair and reasonable, to quote the words that have been used by both Liberal and Conservative prime ministers and ministers of finance. We can only be ready and willing to avail ourselves of any proposals that are fair and reasonable and are not of such a character as will involve injury to this country if they are speedily terminated. I regard that as a factor of the utmost importance, and I believe I always shall, because I never have seen any answer to that argument, whether it be the notice that terminated that reciprocity agreement in 1864 or 1865, or the more recent termination of the Wilson tariff statute.
I can only repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I congratulate the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough for affording the house an op-53719- 143J
portunity to discuss this matter. I have expressed my feeling in that regard, and have given two reasons for that feeling, the one being the historic reason, indicating the willingness of all parties and of this parliament, speaking as parliament, to make agreements that are fair and reasonable and for the good of the people as a whole, and the other argument being that we have been given to understand that within a few months an opportunity will be afforded not to one or two nations but to all the great nations of the world to realize the difficulties that have arisen because of too great reliance having been placed upon nationality as the determining factor in making trade agreements-

Mr. Speaker, in rising to second the resolution which has been so ably moved by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), I wish to congratulate the hon. gentleman on his splendid review of the different negotiations that have taken place in connection with reciprocity, starting in the early days of confederation and continuing to the present time. I think he presented his views in a very impartial and unbiased manner and endeavoured to show as clearly as possible the
Trade with United Slates

benefit? that would accrue to Canada if something of a reciprocal nature could be arranged between the two countries.
I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who has just spoken, did not see fit to tell the house that the government was ready to adopt the resolution, thus making it known to the United States that Canada was willing to trade on reasonable terms, under some carefully worded and carefully thought out trade agreement which would be beneficial to both countries. The right hon. gentleman advanced two reasons as to why this step should not be taken at the present time. The first reason was that in view of the fact that a new government has come into power in the United States it would be premature for Canada to make any advances along this line at the present time. With that argument I cannot agree; I think this is the opportune time for Canada to make a definite pronouncement in this connection. I believe we should let the United States understand that we are perfectly willing to enter into a reciprocal agreement with them if they are willing to meet us on fair and reasonable -terms.
The other argument advanced by the Prime Minister was that in view of the fact that the World economic conference was to be held in the very near future, the matter of tariffs as between Canada and the United States and, for that matter, the world over, might better be left for discussion until that time. He intimated that pending that conference we should not make any pronouncement on the subject. I ask, however, why should not Canada take the lead in this regard? If we believe, as a great proportion of the Canadian people do believe, that there should be lower tariffs, why should not Canada endeavour to take the lead and if possible to make her position clearly felt at that world conference with respect to this important question of reducing tariffs? However, I think we were all glad to see that the Prime Minister was if anything much more reasonable, if I may be permitted to use that term, in his attitude towards tariffs to-day than he has been in the past. There was a time when he told us that he would make the whole world pay tribute to Canada.

At any rate, the right

What do we find when we come to central Canada with our products? We find that the farmers there are producing the very same commodities that we are offering for sale. They are producing butter and cheese, potatoes and vegetables, and they are supplying the cities of Toronto and Montreal, which are the large centres of consumption in this part of the country. The result is that when we look for a market for our products in these centres we are practically shut out.
The difficulty with our farmers at the present time is to find a market. They cannot find a market in those centres which are easily accessible. The United States is the place they can reach with the least difficulty, where therei are water transportation and cheap freight rates to enable them to get the full benefit of the market and to obtain the maximum for their produce. What is the situation with respect to our shipments to Great Britain? As regards the province of Prince Edward Island, our cheese and butter and a great many of our other products have to be loaded on the trains, hauled a distance of seven or eight hundred miles to Montreal, and then loaded on the boat for Great Britain, being taken back past our own door, all of which costs the farmers and the producers of that province a tremendous amount of money. We are three or four thousand miles from the British market and only a few hundred miles from the American, and there are many products we have to sell that are really not required at all in the British market.
The hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough (Mr. Duff) has dealt fully with the fisheries question, which I myself haw brought up in this house on different occasions. Let me refer to it for a moment. Take the question of the shipment of live lobsters. Last season, had it not been for our live lobster trade there would have been really nothing in the fishing season for our fishermen. Our canned goods go largely to the markets of Great Britain, and the price was so low that the fishermen were receiving only 2, 3 and 4 cents per pound for the lobsters that were being packed and
shipped to that market, whereas for their live lobsters going to the United States they were receiving, 15, 20 and often as high as 25 and 30 cents per pound. You can see therefore that if it were not for these shipments of live lobsters to the United States the fishermen of the maritime provinces could scarcely carry on.
As regards the question of lowering tariffs, as I said a moment ago, I am glad to see that the Prime Minister is apparently more favourable to this line of action than he has been in the past. It was my privilege to hear the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin at the Imperial conference, and he made these remarks:
No nation or group of nations, however wealthy and populous, can maintain prosperity in a world where depression and impoverishment reign. Let us therefore aim at the lowering rather than the raising of barriers, even if we cannot fully achieve our purpose now, and let us remember that any action we take here is bound to have its reactions elsewhere.
Mr. Baldwin was plainly of the opinion, even at that conference, where I am sorry to say tariffs were really raised rather than lowered, that the only solution for the problem confronting not only Canada but the world at large was the lowering of tariff barriers if at all possible. With 120.000.000 people right at our doors, is it not natural that we in the maritimes should want to trade with them? Why not try to do business along business lines? Why should this or any otheT government seek to act differently in the negotiating of trade treaties for the extending of trade than would a business man? Business men are afteT business, they try to find markets near at hand and all that this resolution asks for is that similar action be taken by this government.
There is no need to go over all the history from confederation to the present time as it deals with the reciprocity agreements which have been advanced. There is no reason why we should not attempt at the present time to negotiate an agreement better than any agreements negotiated in the past. It is within the possibilities of belief that the present government now coming into power in the United States will be more favourable to trade relations with Canada than have the governments in the past. I think it was during the election campaign that Presidentelect Roosevelt said: Why not let us sit around a table and work out these difficulties; let us start trading with our neighbours in Canada; let us endeavour to get trade moving and then if we can do that we can set our people to work. Sir George W. Ross told his audience that Canadian wheat would lose its identity in passing through the United States and Canada would lose her World markets for that commodity. ward at that time. Sir James Whitney, the Premier of Ontario moved a similar resolution against reciprocity in the Ontario legislature.
This agreement was defeated at the polls in 1911 and I think this constitutes the greatest crime ever committed against the agriculturists of the maritime provinces. Although that offer remained open on the statute books of the United States for ten or twelve years our good Conservative friends here never made any move to accept it even in a modified form that would have met their wishes, and I say emphatically that that is one thing which the people of the maritime provinces hold against the Conservative party. They are responsible for the defeat of the reciprocity agreement. It is due to the neglect of the Conservative party, after the offer had been held open for that period of time by the United States, that no attempt was made to put through even a modified agreement if the agreement as written by Mr. Fielding was not acceptable to the Conservative party. So it is no wonder that the United States then increased her tariffs. The Prime Minister would lead us to believe that the United States was as much to blame as Canada in the matter of increasing tariffs. The United States waited ten or twelve years, and then realizing that Canada apparently had no intention of accepting the treaty in any shape or form, they naturally said to themselves: All we can do is to put up a prohibitory tariff against Canada and shut her goods out of our market. This they proceeded to do, and I say without fear of contradiction that if there is a high tariff imposed by the United States against Canada to-day, a great deal of the blame for that lies at the doors of our friends opposite.
I should like to give a few figures of our exports from the maritimes to the United States and our imports from that country, which strikingly illustrate the nature of the trade we enjoy with the United States. I have picked out just two or three of the most outstanding items. In 1931 we imported from the United States 195,917 hundredweight of potatoes, and in the same year we shipped to the United States 4,594,121 bushels. Of poultry, we imported none from the United States, and we exported to that country 278,480 pounds. Of turnips we imported none from the United States, and we shipped to that country 1,838,829 bushels. Those figures are small compared with our exports in other years. On a great many occasions we have shipped many more millions of bushels to the United States than the figure I have just given. There is one thing I should like the house to realize, and that is that this
5,000,000 bushels of potatoes which we shipped to the United States from the maritimes had to climb over a tariff wall of 75 cents per 100 pounds, and still our friends on the other side of the house ask, what is the use of the American market for the people of the maritimes or for Canada? They ask us, why don't you sell in Toronto and Montreal? Let me tell them that it would take only the shipments from a very few farms in the maritime provinces, given a good year, to completely fill the markets of Toronto and Montreal, and consequently we have to find a larger market than Canada affords.
Notwithstanding that this government promised to do so much for the farmer-they were going to find markets for farm products and blast a way into the markets of the world that were reluctant to receive our products -the best this government can offer us now is to tell the farmers of this country that there is only one thing for them to do, and that is to cut down their production. I say that if ever condemnation could be laid at the door of any government, it should be laid at the door of this government for its suggestion now to the farmers of this country to cut down their production of agricultural and other products.
Our fish products have been referred to by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). We have a very large market for our fresh fish in the United States, in spite of the fact, as the Prime Minister has stated, that there is a duty of two cents a pound against our fish. The Prime Minister said that we could not get our fish into the United States market because it was a low-priced product, but nevertheless, in spite of the duty, we are making very large shipments of fresh fish of various kinds to the United States from the maritimes.

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) did read a letter the other day informing this house that the British government has refused to lift its embargo.
