One would think with figures like these staring hon. members opposite in the face, they would see the error of their way and be willing to reverse their policy in an endeavour to restore to Canada its export trade. They should accept all suggestions from any corner of the house towards reciprocal or other trade arrangements which would benefit not only the trade of Canada and our financial standing but would benefit Canadian farmers. After the mad race for high tariffs which we have witnessed I believe the time has come when this house should consider very carefully every proposal put forward in an endeavour to reach a trade condition which at least to some extent would relieve the Canadian farmers and fishermen.
From an order for return passed by this house a few days ago we learn that 527,000 pounds of New Zealand butter have been admitted into Canada within the last twelve or thirteen months. I see the hon. member opposite in his seat who only a few days ago introduced a resolution asking that something be done by this government for the dairy farmers. I was not surprised when he introduced that resolution, because if ever there was a time when the dairy farmers of Canada required assistance, it is to-day. Notwithstanding the fact that hon. members opposite won the election because of their cry against the Liberal party's policy in connection with New Zealand butter, yet we find in the return to which I have referred that in the short period of only twelve or thirteen months, this large quantity of New Zealand butter has been admitted into Canada. I could give instance after instance of a similar nature, where our friends opposite have neglected to fulfil their promises.
Again I appeal to hon. members opposite not to try to side-track the resolution now before us, not to ask that it be withdrawn, but to give it careful consideration. I suggest that arising from it there should be a treaty which would not have for its purpose the wiping out or injuring of any industry, but rather the improvement of our agriculture and fishing industries. Undoubtedly there are certain commodities people in Canada require which the United States can supply. On the other hand we produce commodities that the United States could use and would be willing to buy from us. As a common sense business proposition, why in the world cannot the people of the United States and
the people of Canada get together on some form of reciprocal agreement which would be beneficial to each country, and benefit particularly the farmers and fishermen of this country?

I believe it is the consensus of opinion that so far as the maritime provinces were concerned that convention or treaty, or whatever you may wish to call it, was of advantage to that section of Canada. off, as happened in 1867. That is one of the reasons why I think the Canadian people in 1911 voted as they did. It may not have been a good reason, but I have no doubt it was a reason.

He believes it to be in the interests of the people of Nova Scotia, particularly the fishing interests, to have access to the New England market. I was bom in sight of American territory, and I have lived all my life there. I represent a constituency which adjoins the American republic on an extensive border line, and I know that propinquity, contiguity, is a strong factor in creating a disposition to trade with our American neighbours, especially between the maritime provinces and New England. Personally I am perfectly willing to enter into an arrangement at any time with respect to that if it can be done on fair and reasonable terms, and terms that will be stable as to time. But I am not willing that we should enter into an arrangement which can be terminated at the whim of any American politician. I spent a week in the gallery of the United States Senate in April, 1929, when the Hawley-Smoot bill was being dealt with in its last stages, and I witnessed what they did and how they handled it. I have no desire to repeat the story here. But there is a large measure of sentiment in both countries ready to consider this question on its merits, and when the proper time arrives, I think we should consider it in that way.

I commend it particularly to the notice of the hon. member for Prince. If he will go back to his constituents and tell them that as long ago as 1879 the government of Sir John A. Let him tell them also of the statement made by Mr. Fielding in 1923. I was a member of the house at the time and recall the circumstances very well. vivendi. I lived for twenty-one years in the constituency of Charlotte, New Brunswick, where they have the largest body of fishermen of any county in New Brunswick, though not as large as some in Nova Scotia. That county particularly, lying as it does along the shores of the bay of Fundy, and adjacent to the American border, is particularly interested in this question. Personally I never could understand why the modus vivendi with respect to the use of our ports was cut off, and I commend the action of the administration in renewing it in the last few days. But I do suggest, in the absence of further information, that the period suggested seems to be too short. I never could understand why it should be limited as to time or as to its operation. I agree entirely with the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough that in the absence of good arguments to the contrary our ports should be open to the Gloucester fishermen not only for shelter and wood and water and repairs but for the privilege of buying bait and supplies and transshipping fish in bond to the American republic. I understand that privilege has been enjoyed at Prince Rupert, British Columbia, for years and years, and why the same principle is not applicable on the Atlantic coast I do not understand. I think some explanation is due. I believe the government will be conferring a benefit upon the fishermen of the Atlantic provinces if they can see their way clear to renewing this modus vivendi for twelve months in the year and allowing the Gloucester fishermen to make those purchases in our ports. I would add, though, that the greatest enemy of the project is not the Canadian government but the supply men of Gloucester, who are absolutely opposed to the distribution of that money in Canada. I shall support this resolution because it discloses evidence of a willingness on our part to remove the restrictions upon trade between the United States and ourselves without adding to the duties on goods imported from other countries. I am heartily in agreement with the speaker who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Vallanee). I am convinced that such an arrangement would be of immense benefit to the wheat growers and cattle raisers of western Canada. Great benefits would accrue if this resolution should receive the support of this house and ultimately become law here and in the United States.
I am exceedingly gratified to see the reception given to the resolution by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). I am sure that the sympathy he has shown towards it will meet with the approval of the whole country. I remember the experience of 1911 when the reciprocity pact then proposed was turned down by the people of Canada. I have always felt that that was a great mistake and that had the people approved it it would have been for the good of Canada and we would have received benefits for all time. I have always felt that that pact was not turned down because of its merits or demerits. Many arguments were advanced by its opponents, but those arguments were more of the nature of a red herring drawn across the trail, an attempt to obscure the fact that the arrangement would be beneficial to Canada as a whole. It was alleged that the existing trade fMr. Vallanee.]
connections would be disrupted, that the trade routes would be changed, that it would have the effect of disturbing the existing transportation systems which had been designed for east and west traffic, that great loss would result to the shareholders in our transportation systems, that our natural resources would be depleted to our harm and to the good of the United States. It was also urged that Canada was rich and did not need reciprocity, that the ties with the mother country would be weakened and ultimately there would be the annexation of Canada by the United States. I do not think there are many hon. members of this house who would fear any one of these supposed dangers today.
We have reached the time when we realize that we need more trade with every country willing to trade with us. The Prime Minister gave expression this afternoon to that view when he said: There is an earnest desire upon the part of the Canadian people to trade with the United States. As Canada turned down the proposed arrangement in 1911 it is perhaps our duty at this time to take the first step in reopening negotiations. I think it would be for the good of Canada that we should make known our wishes with regard to the matter, although it might be better for the government to wait until the new administration is in power in the United States before making formal approaches.
I hope that this resolution may be implemented because I believe it would greatly increase the volume of trade between Canada and the United States to the mutual advantage of both countries. I believe it would lead to a better understanding and a greater appreciation, each of the other, and would tend to eradicate the animosity which has been engendered by the high tariff walls of our respective countries. I believe this is a good time to consider the matter, because on both sides of that imaginary line which is called the boundary between the United States and Canada there is a growing opinion in favour of freer trade between the two countries as well as among other countries of the world. Many men and organizations have been urging that tariff walls should be lowered to permit our trading more freely with each other. I am most heartily in agreement with any suggestion of the kind.
The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the government of Canada reopen negotiations with the government of the United States of America with a view of bringing about a satisfactory reciprocal trade

Trade with United States
arrangement between Canada and the United States whereby the natural products of Canada, that is the products of the sea, the farm, the mine3, and the forests, and including fish, lumber, wheat, cattle, etc., should have free entry into the United States in exchange for the admission of certain goods from the United States of America, which in the interests of both countries may be admitted into Canada, free from customs tariffs.
Surely no hon. member can object to that resolution. It speaks only of arrangements being made which shall be in the interests of both countries. Every hon. member who has the interests of Canada at heart desires that our trade shall increase and unemployment be lessened, and even more so if this can be done without any harm whatsoever to any industry in this country. For these reasons I heartily support the resolution.

I have lived a considerable time in Canada; I have a vivid recollection of the attitude of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house with respect to public questions and reciprocity is one in which I have always been much interested. I know something of its history, and I followed this afternoon the rehearsal of its history by the mover of the resolution (Mr. Duff) and in the remarks made by the leader of the government (Mr. Bennett) with respect to the attitude which the respective political parties had taken on this very important question.
No one will deny for a moment that trade with the United States is the most important in which the Canadian people are engaged. One need only refer to -the annual trade returns issued by government departments to realize that our trade with the United States has always been the most important. Indeed, our trade with the United States and with Great Britain represents about
seventy-five per cent of our total trade, and it has been so for many years.
I shall not recapitulate what has been so well stated this afternoon, by both the mover of the resolution and the leader of the government. I wish rather to base my remarks on events from 1911 onwards. I happened to be in western Canada in 1911, and as one who believed in the utmost freedom of trade and in trade expansion, a cause which I have always espoused and supported, believing that the widest possible measure of trade would be the most beneficial to Canada. I naturally was strongly in favour of the reciprocity treaty. I have never subscribed to the narrower views of trade held by the Conservative party, who believed, and they are entitled to that belief, that the secondary industries were entitled to a certain amount of protection. I believed that it was impossible in any way to lend protection to the great natural industries of this country, our basic industries, lumbering, mining and fishing, upon which the whole success of the commercial fabric of Canada depends, and for that reason I have constantly been opposed to the granting of special privileges which the party opposite have always been willing to extend to secondary industries for their encouragement, and in order, to use their own language, to create a home market for the primary industries of this country. It will be many years before that happy condition of affairs comes about in Canada. I am not forgetting the terrible arraignment which hon. gentlemen now sitting on the treasury benches meted out to us who were then sitting on that side, in speeches much more vitriolic than that made by the right hon. gentleman this afternoon. Many a time it was hurled across the floor of this house that we were only too willing to turn the other cheek when our neighbours to the south saw fit to increase their tariffs against us. But the striking fact remains that throughout all these years in which the tariff controversy has raged, the United States, ever since we have kept trade statistics in this country, has been the best customer for Canadian products. That is the amazing thing, that the United States has remained our best customer, even in face of the exorbitant tariffs enforced by the Americans from time to time against us, tariff increases which made it easy to inflame public opinion in Canada against the United States. It was thought wise in this country to have a great national policy, and hon. gentlemen of the Conservative party talked about "red-blooded Canadianism" if you did

May I say that I was one of those who supported, with all the power I possessed, the reciprocity offer of Mr. Fielding to the United States, believing that despite all the obstacles that had been put in the way of it, the United States was, and still continues to be, the best market for Canadian products. What would it mean if we could remove some of those obstacles? One hon. gentleman has spoken of fish, and another hon. gentleman has spoken of cattle. The removal of those obstacles would mean more than we can estimate. I have not time to go into details, but I know what it would mean to the cattle industry of western Canada. We are trying to sell our cattle to Russia because we have to sell them somewhere, and we cannot sell them in Canada. That is perhaps also one of the vital reasons for our interest in a departure from what is known as sound money, so that wre may sell some of our cattle to Great Britain, as well as other agricultural products. But I emphasize once more that the country to the south, our closest market, is the market we ought to cultivate.
I am surprised for another reason. In the fall session of last year, and only in the fall session, an agreement wfith Great Britain was placed before parliament which members on this side of the house opposed to some extent. We did not oppose the principle contained in the agreement, because it was

directly in line with our policy, but we did oppose the five year guarantee to continue the duties imposed upon certain commodities to be exchanged between Great Britain and Canada. What position would the Prime Minister take? What would he do, in the light of the agreement with Great Britain to which the government has committed Canada for a period of five years? I have all kinds of sympathy for the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) who has spent a considerable time in Paris. I did not know how he could come back with any kind of agreement with France. Why? Some comments are founded on faots, and others on jokes. All I have to say is that if the right hon. gentleman who leads the government is

Trade with United States

sincere in the protestations he made to-day, if he really means now to subscribe to the resolution moved by Mr. Fielding in 1923, I am here to tell him there are many of his followers sitting in this chamber to-night who did not subscribe to it, and who have not changed their position from that time to this. If hon. gentlemen opposite have changed their views, then it is a complete right about face so far as the Conservative party is concerned.
All I have to say is that the more publicity that is given to the resolution before us, the better for Canada. If it will increase trade- because heaven knows there is nothing we need worse-certainly it would be of great benefit to the country. If ever I had any doubts about the position I have taken concerning trade matters, oertainly they have been dispelled within the last year and a half or two years. Hon. gentlemen opposite have demonstrated beyond peradventure that by their trade policies they can ruin the country quicker than by any other course they could pursue. If hon. members do not believe what I say, I ask them to look at the trade returns. Where are we going? Where are we to get the revenue with which to pay our indebtedness? Where are we to get the money to meet the ordinary running expenses of the country? I have much sympathy for my good friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). No man in the government is entitled to more sympathy than he, because one of these days he will have to make a rather sorry statement to the House of Commons concerning the revenue of the country.
The quicker we revive trade and the quicker this suicidal policy of the Conservative party is changed to one of reciprocity with people who are willing to trade with us, the better it will be for Canada. I could not sit stall in my seat and observe without comment the sudden change of front shown by the government. We were to have an announcement which, we understood, would startle us, but nothing could startle me more than the statement I heard to-day; nothing could appeal to me more. I expected an entirely different statement.
If we approach the United States showing that we are unwilling, as the party opposite has demonstrated in the past, to give any concessions that will injure Canadian industry- and I mean secondary industries, because the Lord knows we cannot injure the primary industries-if we go with the avowed intention of having extreme protection, I have very little faith in the result of any trade arrangements we may try to make with the United
fMr. C. A. Stewart.]
States. In my view any trade agreement on that basis with Great Britain can be of very little benefit, and to prove my contention I would ask any hon. member to look at the current trade statistics. The figures will indicate that the improvement in trade with Great Britain is so small it is hardly noticeable. If the government approached the United States with a fixed policy of that kind in mind, the possibilities of reciprocity would be very small indeed. But, I believe in spite of everything that can be done, in spite of the high tariff forces in the United States, in spite of the high tariff forces in Canada, our trade with the United States will increase. Perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite, after three years of trial of a high tariff policy, will be willing to listen to reason. Perhaps they will be willing to offer something worth while towards the improvement of trade conditions.

Mr. Speaker, it would1 appear to
me as an. ordinary onlooker that there must be considerable disappointment in the ranks of the hon. gentleman's friends. It is quite evident that all the speeches that we have been listening to this afternoon from that side were prepared with the expectation that the government was going to oppose the resolution of my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). They show a persistent attempt to create the impression in the country that this government is opposed to reciprocal relations with the United States. Now I come from the province of Nova Scotia, the proudest province of the dominion, where there is a tradition in favour of reciprocity with the United States. It was said by Joseph Howe many years ago that if you were to throw a board on the waters of Nova Scotia it would float to Boston. In those early days before confederation there was a great trade between the maritime provinces, particularly Nova Scotia and Boston. Fishing vessels from Boston, Provincetown and the other New England ports always came to Nova Scotia-including the little village in which I was bom-and fitted out, shipped men and materials, and came back in the fall and discharged their crews. Many of the crews went to Boston during the winter months, and shortly afterwards their families followed them, with the result that to-day in the New England states there are more people of Nova Scotia parentage than there are in the province of Nova Scotia itself.
From the discussion this afternoon it is quite clear that both parties are in favour of this resolution. Let me say right here that I am not in favour of it in the terms in which it is expressed. There is no doubt that many years ago Nova Scotia enjoyed great prosperity owing to the freedom of trade that existed between it and the New England states. But things are different to-day. We sometimes make the mistake of thinking that 53719-1445
if we could return to the days of our fathers and grandfathers we would enjoy the same prosperity that they did. Such is not the case. I doubt whether the fishermen of Gloucester and Provincetown and Boston are much more prosperous to-day than our own fishermen are. It must be remembered that the fish business has gone down all over the world. It has certainly gone down in the maritime provinces. During the past few years we have tried to build up a fresh fish business with upper Canada. For this purpose trawlers have been licensed; out on the banks they keep in daily touch by wireless with the merchants, thus ensuring a continuous supply of fresh fish from Nova Scotia to the Toronto and Montreal markets. It is urged that they have been the death of the shore fisherman'-with that I will deal later- but just let me ask you what would happen to that fresh fish business if the bars were let down and fresh fish landed from vessels sailing out of Gloucester and Boston appeared in the Montreal and Toronto markets. It is true that the shore fishermen throughout the lower provinces have suffered; I do not think that anywhere in the country there is greater destitution and suffering than among the fishermen of the maritime provinces. I am in agreement with my hon. friend from Antig-onish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) on one point,, and that is the great desirability of the modus vivendi. I believe that American fishing vessels should be permitted to enter maritime province ports to tranship their fish, purchase their supplies, make all necessary repairs and ship men if necessary. That would give our shore fishermen an opportunity to make a living which they do not now enjoy. I could tell you stories of shore fishermen who pursue that hardy calling, going out to sea in the early morning, returning with their boatload of fish, and being obliged either to sell them for one cent apiece or to throw them away. With proper cold storage facilities the fishermen could put those fish away for bait and so get a reasonable living. In this connection I might mention that we have storage facilities at North Sydney and Sydney Harbour, but these have been practically destroyed so that they are of absolutely no use to the fishermen. With such facilities as these afforded, however, the town of North Sydney would prosper.
There is one point to which I should direct the attention of my hon. friend. Among other things his resolution includes the natural products of Canada, the products of the sea, the farm, the forests and the mines. I wonder how long the coal mines of Nova Scotia would
Trade with United Stales

last if we had reciprocity with regard to coal. Their destruction would be very sudden and very complete. I venture to believe that this great industry in Nova Scotia, upon which one-fifth of our population depends for a livelihood, would disappear in a few years. Therefore I am obliged to take issue with my hon. friend on that point, though as far as fish go I am at one with him.

Mr. Speaker, I deem it
my duty to express the views of those who I have the honour of representing in the house- the farmers of Laprairie-Napierville-on this all important question introduced by the resolution of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). The resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the government of Canada reopen negotiations with the government of the United States of America with a view of bringing about a satisfactory reciprocal trade arrangement between Canada and the United States whereby the natural products of Canada, that is the products of the sea, the farm, the mines, and the forests, and including fish, lumber, wheat, cattle, etc., should have free entry into the United States in exchange for the admission of certain goods from the United States of America, which in the interests of both countries may be admitted into Canada, free from customs tariffs.
To summarize, this motion requests the renewal of the treaty negotiated by the Liberal party, in 1911, in order to promote wider trade relations with our neighbours to the south. I need not mention that the Quebec farmers, especially those located on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, close to the United States frontier are, and have always been, in favour of a reciprocal trade treaty. Indeed the people of Laprairie-Napierville and those of the counties bordering on the United States, would greatly benefit from such a treaty. Producers of milk, butter and cream, who are numerous in these counties, under a fair tariff, compared with the one our friends opposite recently enacted, sold at a profit their milk products to the United States. If such an agreement could be concluded between the two countries, there is no doubt that our farmers would find, in the United States, a market which would improve their condition, especially in these times of depression. The same may be said about the farmers who specialize in wheat and hay. A number of western members and all those interested in the live stock trade have sufficiently threshed out this question, I need not, therefore further insist.

The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) stated, this afternoon, that one of the main reasons why he opposed reciprocity, in 1911, was that the treaty could be terminated without notification. I do not see how the right hon. Prime Minister could oppose this resolution for such a trivial reason, because now that he is in power he can amend, as he pleases, this resolution and add a clause stipulating that in case one of the contracting parties washed to end this treaty, a notice should be given.
The right hon. Prime Minister further stated that our two great political parties have had this question before them ever since 1879, and have always favoured a reciprocal treaty with our neighbours to the south; he also added that, as the two parties agreed on this resolution, the mover should, in the interest of the country withdraw his motion, and not insist that a vote be taken. I find it hard to understand why the members opposite would oppose this resolution simply because it might bring on a vote which would divide the house into two adverse camps. I have some notions of logic, yet I cannot quite grasp how the people's representatives, in the house, can possibly be in favour of a measure and when a vote is taken refuse to support it.
May I request the right hon. Prime Minister to explain how it is possible for him to be both for and against this resolution.
He will permit me, however, to remind him of the speeches he made, when he first came out as a candidate in the Dominion election of 1911. We have but to refer to the press despatches of that date to ascertain how strenuously the Calgary candidate opposed the reciprocity treaty with the United States. One of the main arguments invoked to justify his opposition was, that if this measure carried, the empire would be destroyed, the spirit of loyalty existing in Canada would be crushed; he did not wish to trade with the United States, because this would be an act of disloyalty. And how many other arguments did he invoke! After being elected, he had the honour of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and the following are his words on the reciprocal trade treaty:
Mr. Speaker, in that portion of this great Dominion in which I am privileged to reside, a very substantial portion of our population has come from the great republic to the south, and one of the strongest reasons I had for opposing the reciprocity agreement was that it threw into the melting pot for solution a question that involved a problem in patriotism. When we remember that so large a portion of our population came from that great republic, where they

Trade with United States
inherited traditions that were at least not favourable to monarchial institutions; when they learned through the medium of the American press, that, however much their former political parties differed with each other, they showed unanimity in favour of these proposals, and when they found American public men preaching a doctrine that indicated that the consequences of this agreement would be the absorption of western Canada at least by the great republic, and at all events rendering impossible for all time the commercial and organic union of those overseas dominions and the motherland which comprise the British Empire, it was little wonder that these people allied themselves with those who were in favour of the reciprocity pact.
Having read the speeches delivered by the then representative for Calgary-now the Prime Minister of Canada-on the hustings and in the house, we are rather agreeably surprised to note what are his views on this question to-day. The right hon. Prime Minister has greatly changed his views since those days when Laurier compared his speeches to the turbulent wafers of the Bow river. Evidently he shows that he is intelligent, which no one has ever doubted. I am a Liberal, however, I am not so narrowminded as to think that nothing good can come from outside the Liberal ranks. No one in this house will recognize more readily than I do that the Prime Minister is steering in the direction of liberalism. Although I do not expect that he will join our ranks, I can assert that he is not one of those mentioned by Lady Asquith who stated that only the gods and fools do not alter their views. I can assert here, and pay him the compliment, that he is neither in one nor the other of these classes, notwithstanding the fact that a large number of his one-sided followers have so exalted him that they sometimes have looked upon him as a god. The right hon. Prime Minister has this afternoon brought them to earth by informing them that he has altered his views since 1911, that he is neither a god nor a fool.
As to us, sir, we have no need of changing our views on the subject, and no one will ever blame us for it, especially when we witness members opposite view this question of trade reciprocity in the same light as we do. I am doubly in favour of this resolution because I note by the change faking place opposite towards our own views, that we are still more assured of being in the right path.
I therefore trust that this resolution will receive the unanimous support of the house. Let hon. gentlemen opposite not fall into the error of resorting to such tactics as contending that they approve of the resolution,
but not in its present form. Let them not blunder by opposing this resolution; let them prove their patriotism by voting unanimously in favour of this resolution, so that the government in power across the border be made aware, once for all, that the reciprocal trade treaty is not a dead letter in our statutes, but is always and more than ever a living issue, and, that the moment the United States will show their willingness to act, they will find on this side of the frontier people who will welcome their proposals and say: We are ready to negotiate a reciprocal treaty with you on products of the land and sea, and also those that can be exchanged to the mutual benefit of the two parties interested.
I shall close my remarks, sir, by stating that everything prompts me to hope that the right hon. Prime Minister, as well as his followers, will continue to show that they are intelligent, farsighted and wise by unanimously voting for this resolution,

I closely followed the reply of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). Briefly, it means that we cannot have a reciprocal treaty with the United States because, first, our neighbours to the south would have to lower their tariff, and our government is unable to force them to take such a step. My reply to the right hon. Prime Minister is that it was himself wrho, last summer, was responsible for the agreements concluded with the British commonwealth. Since he displayed his great ability in bringing about a trade treaty with the British commonwealth, he might do the same to obtain from the United States government what the Liberal party has often attempted: to negotiate a reciprocal treaty.
In 1911, the Liberal party did negotiate such a treaty with the United States, but unfortunately, this famous treaty was rejected by the people. Had the Liberal party been maintained in power, in 1911, I am convinced that Canada would have been better served. Moreover, the great majority of the people admit, today, that had the treaty been ratified Canada would have made great strides along the path of prosperity.
Trade with United States

Our country had a few years of such prosperity from 1921 to 1929, however, after the Tories returned to power business declined and prosperity gave way to depression.
The hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough did not wish to introduce politics into this question, this afternoon. He simply requested the government to use its good offices in order to negotiate a reciprocal treaty, especially in connection with the fisheries of Canada. I shall support this motion and I trust the right hon. Prime Minister will enter into negotiations with the United States in order to obtain reciprocal arrangements in tariff matters. The United States will certainly not lower their duty on fish unless we are ready to grant them reciprocal advantages. May I point out to the house that our fish industry has been in a deplorable state for a number of years. Not only are we unable to export our fish, but when we wish to import the necessary fishing equipment, such as nets, marine motors, etc., we have to contend with too high a tariff. If we are willing to lower our tariff on marine motors and all fishing equipment entering Canada from the United States, I think the latter will grant us, in return, concessions on our fish.
The only way to bring back prosperity is to conclude a trade treaty with the United States. As long as the Conservative government maintains its 1930 tariff, prosperity will not return to us. I therefore beseech the right hon. Prime Minister not to reject the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), but to give it his serious consideration, and therefore, I trust the house will unanimously vote in favour of this resolution.

The government must act to relieve the present situation of the farming classes and thus avoid a general bankruptcy.
Because of the present crisis, we should set aside party differences and endeavour to save the situation. I therefore think that the best way to do so, would be to negotiate a reciprocal trade treaty with the United States.

The people of Canada would be very grateful to the government if it brought back to the farming classes the prosperity they enjoyed under the liberal regime. The slightest improvement in our trade relations with our neighbours would mean more to us than all the agreements signed at the Imperial Economic Conference of 1932.
I believe that some of the members of this administration will be forced, by circumstances, to cast their vote in favour of this motion.
I shall quote what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) stated in the house, at page 692 of Hansard, on October 25, 1932:
I would also draw the attention of the leader of the opposition to this fact, that the strongest argument brought against the reciprocity pact of 1911 was that it was to continue for only one year. That is what defeated that pact, and we know what happened to the Liberal party on that occasion.
The hon. gentleman stated that if, in 1911, reciprocity was defeated, it was because we requested a treaty for one year only. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in connection with this resolution. As I understand it, the resolution suggests the reopening of negotiations with the United States to arrange if possible a reciprocal pact for the exchange of the natural products of this country for certain products of the United States. It is an effort to procure wider markets, and our trade returns clearly show that wider markets are badly needed. Canadian imports in 1929 were valued at $1,265,000,000; in 1932 they had dwindled to $578,000,000. Taking the value in 1926 as the basis, the volume would be represented by $1,403,000,000 and $808,000,000 respectively. In 1929 the exports of Canada were valued at $1,363,000,000 and in 1932 they had dwindled to $576,000,000. We find that the volume of exports of agricultural products has diminished from 129 to 72.4. Surely it is evident that wider markets are needed for our Canadian products.
A few weeks ago the news went abroad that there was a possibility of selling some of our Canadian cattle in Russia. That news reached the ears of men in this country who are vitally interested in the cattle business, and many of us who represent western constituencies have received numerous letters from men who are anxious to sell their cattle. Of course, it was realized that this government could not guarantee profits or accept Russian bonds, but it was felt that there was a market for cattle in Russia and they hoped that some way would be found by which some of our surplus stock could reach that market. Nothing more clearly indicates the desire of the primary producers of Canada to find a market; nothing more clearly indicates the need of such a market, and these people are looking to the members of this parliament for some solution of their problem.
Someone has said that we should not go to Mr. Roosevelt with our hat in our hand to beg for an agreement. I think the Canadian people will agree with that, but they realize also that a salesman does not wait in his office for orders to come in. Surely Canadians are not bankrupt as far as salesmanship is concerned. Surely, when they have a great surplus to dispose of, they will not hesitate to try to find a market for it. This resolution deals particularly with primary products, and we all know that the prosperity of Canada as a whole depends upon the prosperity of those in the primary industries. IVe know that the curve marking the general business follows the curve which indicates the activity in the agricultural industry. That being so, it is of the greatest importance to the people of Canada as a whole that they should have a prosperous agricultural industry. It is true that in making agreements we cannot expect to get all the advantages. Some of our secondary industries may have to be sacrificed. But if that is true, is it not also true that those industries are failing in any case? Is it not so that as the days go by and we make little progress in solving our problems, industry after industry in Canada is failing to balance its budget, as it were-failing even to earn the interest on its bonds? So that the larger considerations must first receive the attention of this house.
The district whence I come was once one of the great ranching districts of Canada. Later the ranches were broken up as settlers came in, and to-day those great areas are
Trade with United States

vacant. If there was a market for our cattle those areas would be used for ranching purposes, but the few ranchers who have thus far survived are finding it extremely difficult to carry on, and if present conditions continue they, too, will have to give up. As an illustration I might point out that one junction which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) knows well, the junction of Dunmore, once shipped thousands and thousands of cattle, and to-day the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is asking permission to have that station closed. Nothing more clearly indicates the fate which has befallen the ranching industry in that country. Their great market was in the United States, but changes in the American tariffs have shut off that great market.
I wish to put on record a few figures which will indicate what the various American tariffs have done to this great Canadian industry. From October 3, 1913, to May 27, 1921, the United States under the Underwood tariff allowed our cattle to enter that country free, and what do we find? We find that in the year 1920, 420,891 cattle entered the United States. Then on May 27, 1921, the United States imposed an emergency tariff of thirty per cent against our cattle, which tariff remained in force until September 21, 1922. At once we see that, instead of shipping some 400,000 cattle, to the United States our exports dropped to 224,000. Then on September 21, 1922, the Fordney-McCumber tariff came into force and at once there was a further drop in our exports, so that in 1925 we shipped only 123,438 head to the United States. The last blow came on June 18, 1930, when the Hawley-Smoot tariff came into operation. That tariff levies a duty on cattle, of less than 700 pounds, of 21 cents a pound, and of 3 cents a pound on cattle over 700 pounds. In the year ending June 30, 1932, our exports of cattle to the United States dropped to 18.651. Nothing more clearly illustrates the advantage of that great market than the fact that we have suffered so much when it has been closed to us.
Of course I realize that it is not within the power of the members of this house to open that American market. On the other hand the responsibility of governments for the welfare of its citizens has been fully established, and an effort might and should be made to get us into that market at least under more favourable terms than we can enter it at present. Years have passed since any active effort has been made in that direction, but 1 believe that, especially at this time, if a real effort was made in a businesslike way it would

bring some measure of hope and courage to men who are at the present time most discouraged .

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I closely followed the remarks made this afternoon by the right hon. Prime Minister, on the resolution before the house.
To my mind this resolution purports to lay down the principle that a reciprocal trade treaty between the United States and Canada is desirable. We have witnessed a most amazing change in the views of the leader of the government. However, in order to explain his present attitude, he referred to Canadian history as far back as 1865, the year our reciprocal treaty with the United States was abrogated. After this event the Conservative party which held power in 1879, adopted, it seems, a measure endorsing the policy of reciprocity with the United States. This measure purported to allow free entry into Canada of a large number of products from the United States the moment the latter country reciprocated those advantages. Again this policy was endorsed by the Conservative party in 1888. In 1890 and 1894, however, it was slightly modified, that is, the reciprocity policy was extended to all other countries which offered us the same privileges.
This is somewhat the stand taken by the Conservative party, judging from the speech of the right hon. Prime Minister, as regards our trade relations with the United States. He also referred to the attitude of the Liberal party from 1897 to 1911, on trade matters. There were but slight changes, it seems, in the acts of 1897, 1904, 1910 and even 1911, and, according to the Prime Minister we are led to believe the two parties, in connection with external trade, advocated the same policy.
May I, sir, endeavour to prove that with the same policies we do not beget the same results. In 1911, the Liberal party, after recognizing the principle of reciprocity, adopted a measure allowing the free entry into Canada of numerous products, while the United States adopted a similar measure. Then the election of 1911 took place. Although advocating the same policy, as it seems, the Conservative party endeavoured to defeat this reciprocal trade treaty, or rather defeat the two measures, and their battle horse was: "No truck nor trade with the Yankees." In 1911, the Conservative party, therefore, denied-and we blamed them for it, at the time-the policy advocated by Cartier and Macdonald, in 1879, 1888, and the other years when measures tending to the same

Trade with United States
results were enacted. The Conservative party succeeded in convincing the majority of the people that they were right, and the people voted down the reciprocity treaty with the United States after winning the election, notwithstanding the fact that the Democrats were still in power in the United States, no steps were ever taken by the Conservative party to put into force these acts.
In 1923, under the Liberal regime, efforts were made to bring about such reciprocal arrangements but no results followed-I think that the Republican party was then in power. In a few days the United States will have at the helm of affairs the Democratic party which on many scores resembles the Liberal party, especially as regards their tariff policy. Is it the advent to power of this party which has brought about such a change in the Prime Minister's views on trade intercourse with the United States? He has, however, for eveT so long, known what was the trend of trade with our neighbours to the south as shown in the statistics, and also that with other nations. He is fully aware that, even with our high tariff protection, our trade with the United States represents half of our total trade with the entire world and the two-thirds of our trade with foreign countries. Our trade with the United States is twice as large as that with the British Empire. He is fully aware that notwithstanding all tariff restrictions and obstacles, it was impossible for us not to trade with United States.
The right hon. Prime Minister referred to our geographical situation. If it is true that this geographical situation lends itself to trade intercourse with the United States is it not much more natural to trade with them than with distant countries.
I doubt very much whether this so long delayed repentance on the part of the Prime Minister can have practical results in connection with our trade with the United States. What has been the Conservative party's tariff policy with our neighbours, since it assumed power, in 1930? They increased the customs duties on two-thirds of our tariff items, contending that the Fordney-McCumber and Hawley-Smoot tariffs, necessarily obliged us to adopt such a policy. It was laying down the principle that the tariff was to be used as a threat rather than as a means of trading.
We must, however, note with joy this acknowledgment by the Prime Minister, because we, the Liberal party, are convinced that we shall only return to prosperity by increasing our trade with the United States, as well as with the other countries.
When you raise a tariff barrier between Canada and the United States, you hinder trade, whether it be imports or exports. When I examine our trade statistics for 1931,
I find that we are making a great blunder in refusing to trade with the United States, notwithstanding their prohibitive tariff, because in	1931, our exports to the
nations comprising the British Commonwealth amounted to $292,884,145, and our imports were $204,935,168; while our exports to foreign lands, in those countries which also have a high tariff wall against us, amounted to $506,768,522 and our imports to $701,677,513. This proves that our trade outside the empire is far larger than within the empire.
It took our government two years to negotiate a pact with Uie British Commonwealth. Why should it not now endeavour to negotiate trade conventions with the other countries? Our agreements with the various nations of the British Commonwealth will always appear as an impediment, however, even then, I think that an honest and sincere effort on the part of our government would produce good results. I fear that, not having the same policy as the Domocrats in tariff matters, our government may encounter some opposition from our neighbours to the south, however the effort will not harm us.
I have but one further argument to set forth, before closing my remarks. The Prime Minister, in a meek and very conciliating mood, requested the sponsor to withdraw his resolution. His party was well disposed to negotiate with the United States. It was better not to bring on any clash between the two parties in the house. In due time, he would take the necessary course to open up trade negotiations with the United States. If the policy submitted to the house is to the advantage of Canada, if the principle of reciprocity is sound, there is no need for the sponsor of this resolution to withdraw it. If it is desired to show a united front before the country, the United States and the other countries, this resolution should be unanimously carried, thus the house would give a proof of its sincerity. I am aware that our friends opposite hailing from Quebec will find it hard to vote for this trade and policy, they who, in 1911, 1917, 1921, 1925, 1926 and 1930, boasted of the contrary throughout Quebec; however, it is never too late to repent. I think that they would rise in the people's esteem by adopting the principle of this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, We in the maritime provinces, all things being equal, would be quite in favour of the
Trade with United States

resolution now under consideration. For generations our natural market has been down the Atlantic seaboard in the New England states. We always found a profitable market there, and while that market remained open to us we in the maritime provinces were very prosperous indeed. My idea of the tariff situation to-day is that tariffs throughout the world,-in America, Europe or wherever you may go-are much too high. To my mind they constitute a great restraint upon the trade and commerce between countries.
Hon. gentlemen opposite who spoke this afternoon appear to have tried to convey the impression to the house and the country- and more- particularly the country-that the tariffs imposed against us by the United States are of our own making. They would try to have us believe that the tariffs against our goods entering the United States were made in Ottawa. Such, however, is not the case. Those tariffs are made in Washington, and anything that this parliament has been able to do or say has not had the effect of lowering their tariffs. The hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) spoke about the decline of trade between Canada and the United States. True, trade has declined, but while trade will decrease or increase very quickly according to the prices of the different commodities concerned, a decline in value does not always indicate a decline in volume. That is one point which should not be forgotten. However there has 'been a very good reason for the decrease in trade in the last two years between Canada and the United States.
After six o'clock I managed to secure some figures concerning a few of the commodities with which I am most concerned, and I should like to place them on Hansard to show what has happened during the last few years. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) spoke about the cattle trade, and made reference to the great trade enjoyed until the year 1921 between the western prairie provinces and the United States. Why should there not have been that trade? Up to 1921 Canadian cattle entered the American market free of duty, and I am of the opinion they should still enter under the same condition; we all believe that. However, in 1930 conditions were different. As the hon. member stated, cattle of 700 pounds or under were subjected to duty of two and a half cents a pounds while on cattle over 700 pounds the duty was three cents per pound. Again, take poultry; in 1921 the United States duty was one cent a pound; in 1930 it was 8 cents a pound. It was intended that the duty should be prohibitive; that is why it was put on. On sheep, which entered the United States

free in 1921, you now have to pay $3 per head, almost half the price of the sheep. Oats that in 1921 entered the United States at 6 cents for thirty-two pounds now pay 16 cents -prohibitive again. Wheat, which was free in 1921, now pays 42 cents per bushel. Wheat flour, which was free in 1921, now pays SI.04 a barrel. Pork, something in which we are all interested-in our section of the country vitally so, for it is one of the chief articles of export-in 1921 was free of duty; to-day it pays 3| cents a pound to enter the American market. Butter in 1921 carried a duty of 2J cents a pound. I would not complain about that, but imagine a duty on butter in 1930 of 14 cents a pound, almost the price of the article! Cheese in 1920 was 20 per cent ad valorem; now it is 35 per cent. Cream, which was free-and this should interest the farmers of central Canada-now pays 56.6 cents per gallon, a duty intended to be prohibitive and nothing else. Potatoes, in which we, in our province, are vitally interested, were free in 1921; now we have to pay a duty of 75 cents per hundred pounds to get them into the United States. Turnips, another article that we export largely, were 15 per cent then1; they are now 25 cents per hundred pounds. So it is easy to see why the trade between Canada and the United- States should decline, under the duties I have mentioned, duties which were clearly meant to be prohibitive.
But just as the exports from Canada to the United States have declined, we are pleased to be able to inform this house that owing to the beneficial arrangements made at the Imperial economic conference held here last August, our exports to British countries are on the increase. During the last six months of 1932 our exports to the United Kingdom totalled 8116,487,568 as against 8102,433,809 for -the first half of the year, an increase of $13,953,759. That is where our exports are going now. We have found the United States market very fickle, and I believe that is what the Canadian exporter is afraid of. We want markets upon which we can -rely over a long period of -time. It is no light matter for an exporter to establish connections in a certain country and build up the shipping facilities necessary to move his product, and then have his exports to that country ruthlessly dhut off overnight, as was done by the United States in 1930.
The same is true of Canada's exports to other British dominions. During the last six months of 1932 our exports to empire countries totalled $137,209,418 compared with $126,483,054 for the same period of 1931, a gain in the year of $10,726,364.

Trade with 'Jnited States
Now my Eon. friend from Prince (Mr. MacLean) made some statements tihiis afternoon with reference to the export of potatoes. He told us, I think, that somewhere around
4,000,000 bushels of potatoes had been exported, largely from the maritime provinces, even in spite of the 75 cents per hundred pounds duty. My hon. friend was a little in error there, because in the year he refers to the duty on potatoes was only 50 cents a bushel. I remember quite well the fight that took place with reference to this duty on potatoes in 1929. I happened at that time to be a director of the Prince Edward Island Potato Growers' Association. Foolishly, I now think, we spent a considerable sum of money in conjunction with men and firms in the southern states who were buying our potatoes; we had men at Washington looking after our interests; we did all that men could do to prevent the United States from raising that duty on our potatoes from 50 cents to 75 cents. Our effort was absolutely in vain. The state of Maine and other potato growing localities of New England simply brushed us aside; they had their way, and the duty was put at 75 cents per one hundred pounds.
Now we are just as anxious to trade with the United States as they are to trade with us. Figures have been given here to-day about the great volume of export business that we had with the United States up to a year or two ago. That business now is to a certain extent shut off. I imagine that the American people will miss that business, and they will now be more ready to listen to us regarding a reduction in tariffs than they would have been had we allowed that business to flow freely over our borders. I think we have given them a little check-up and taught them a lesson, and I believe that with the new government to be inaugurated in Washington, representing the Democratic party, who have always appeared to be a lower tariff party, we shall soon be able to arrange some nice little bargains with them in reference to the interchange of goods, especially products of the farm, the sea, and the forest.
A good deal has been said here to-day about that famous 1011 reciprocity election. I remember it very well. I took a considerable part in it in support of the candidates who were contesting the constituency I now have the honour to represent. The result of that election was no snap verdict. I do not remember any question that was more clearly and fully put to the Canadian electors, and more fully explained to them than was that reciprocity pact during the campaign of 1911. I imagine it was some time in late March
or early April that Mr. Fielding, the Minister of Finance at the time, came back from Washington with that agreement. It was announced here in the House of Commons, it was published in the Canadian press; from one end of this country to the other, speakers on both sides of politics went out and fully explained the matter to the electors. And vou must take this further fact into consideration, that for fifteen long years the Conservative party had been in hopeless opposition.
I say "hopeless" because some of the Conservatives we tried to persuade to cling to the old Tory banner were becoming discouraged, and we were almost discouraged ourselves. I do not see how the defeat of the reciprocity pact of 1911 ever can be blamed on the Conservative party. It is quite true that Conservative politicians and candidates did their best to explain to the Canadian people that it would not be good for them to enter into that agreement, but it is equally true that my hon. friend the late Minister of Justice and his colleagues went the length and breadth of this country in support of that proposal, using great eloquence and taking full advantage of the fact that at their head they had a loved leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who until that day never had tasted defeat. That is quite an asset to any party. Those were the conditions, and if there is any fault to be found with the verdict that was rendered on that occasion I do not see that the blame should rest with the Conservative party. The old Tories voted as they always had voted, so there must have been a lot of Liberals who turned over and voted against the reciprocity pact. Therefore the credit or discredit, depending on how you look at it, for the defeat of that pact belongs to the Liberal voters.	.
I do not intend to take up much more of the time of the house on this question. I was a little surprised this afternoon to hear my hon. friend from Prince mention butter; I thought that was the one question upon which he would not have touched. My hon. friend mentioned the live lobster industry of Prince Edward Island; he spoke of it in such a tone of voice that one would almost think there was some great obstacle in the way of shipping those lobsters to the United States. My hon. friend knows very well that live lobsters enter the United States free of duty, so there is no reason why we should not do a good, profitable business in that line. My hon. friend, however, bemoaned the fact that during the present year we have imported some 350,000 pounds of New Zealand butter. Why, Mr. Speaker, that would not butter very many slices of bread. Last year we manufactured
Trade with United States

within our own borders some 300,000,000 pounds of butter, almost all of which was consumed in Canada, so it will be seen that 350,000 pounds would not be a drop in the bucket. It is quite true that the price of butter was low last summer; I regret that fact as much as anyone could regret it because that is the way I make my living. But just think what would have happened if hon. gentlemen opposite had been in power and that famous New Zealand agreement had been in force, under which from 30,000,000 to 54,000,000 pounds of butter annually was allowed into Canada to flood our market.
I have no quarrel with the resolution now before the house. I confess quite freely and frankly that the people of the maritime provinces, and I believe the people of the dominion generally, are anxious indeed to trade with the United States. That is quite natural, because they are our nearest neighbours, but there is no use in my trying to sell a horse to my neighbour if he does not want to buy it. Before I can do business I must look for someone who needs a horse and is able to buy it. I would be the last man on earth to accuse my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guys-borough (Mr. Duff) of doing anything in an underhand way; I know he would not do that, but I have an idea that hon. gentlemen opposite have taken into consideration the fact that the Prime Minister so ably piloted Canada through the Ottawa conference and arrived at trade agreements which within the next three or four years cannot help but make agriculture in this country prosperous; I am afraid they feared that the right hon. gentleman might do the same thing again and arrive at a beneficial agreement with the United States. To my mind this resolution is advanced at this time more or less to forestall any action of that kind on the part of the Prime Minister. If that be the object of the resolution I should feel like voting against it, but if it was advanced in an honest desire to secure a trade agreement between Canada and the United States I should be very happy to support it.
Mr. F. H. PICKEtL (Brome-Missisquoi): Mr. Speaker, this resolution reads:
.. .it is expedient that the government of Canada reopen negotiations with the government of the United States of America with a view of bringing about a satisfactory reciprocal trade arrangement between Canada and the United States whereby the natural products of Canada, that is the products of the sea, the farm, the mines and the forests, and including fish, lumber, wheat, cattle, etc., should have free entry into the United States in exchange for the admission of certain goods from the United States of America...

I want to say right here, Mr. Speaker, that as far as products of the farm are concerned I am absolutely against any reciprocal arrangement with the United States. If we had reciprocity with the United States to-day we would get five cents a pound less for our butter and seven cents a dozen less for our eggs. Do hon. gentlemen opposite understand that? To-day Canadian farm produce commands the highest prices paid anywhere on earth. That does not include beef, but I would tell western members that beef is going to bring a better price; we have concluded a trade arrangement with Great Britain which eventually will provide a good market for our beef.
With regard to fish, lumber and cattle, if some arrangement could be made by which these commodities could be admitted to the United States I would be very much in favour of it, but certainly such an arrangement would hurt us if it included the products of the farm, and I shall have to vote against the resolution for that reason. Since last August, when for the first time in a good many years Canadian farm produce commanded better prices than were paid in the United States, I have expected advances to be made with regard to reciprocity, but I did not expect those advances to come from the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). I thought they would come from the United States. This takes me back a great many years. I am older than most members of this house, and I live within striking distance of the American line, so I know how our people have been treated. The treaty we had with the United States was abrogated in 1865 and for several years, until 1878 or 1879, the farmers of Canada took 10 cents a pound for their butter, 5 cents for eggs and 5 cents for cheese, while the Americans were laughing at us. Their attitude was, "If you want to participate in the advantages of our markets, join us". I know what I am talking about.
In 1879 we brought down a national policy. At that time we did no manufacturing in Canada but depended upon foreign markets, principally the United States and England, for manufactured goods. We brought down a tariff, and I want to say right here that there are only two industries that have been uninterruptedly well protected since 1879, namely, tobacco and rubber. Where are those industries to-day? They are both flourishing, and I contend that if all our industries had had good, sane, reasonable and continuous protection they would also be flourishing today.

Trade with United Slates
I have been amused as well as perplexed by the logic of the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) who is a free trader. I have heard him on two or three occasions in this house, the last time just before adjournment, extolling the healthy and enviable position of the rubber industry in Canada. I wonder what that hon. gentleman thinks the healthy and enviable position of the rubber industry is due to. Is it due to free trade? Well, they have had a steady 35 per cent protection since 1879. From 1879 until 1885 or 1886 I could save my return fare on the railway going twenty miles to Richford, Vermont, in buying two pairs of rubbers. We began to establish rubber factories, commencing with one in the county adjoining me, the county of Granby. We built the Miner factory, the Granby, the Dominion, the Hamilton, the Gutta Percha, the Goderich, the Goodyear, Jacques Cartier, and other rubber concerns, and to-day all these rubber companies are competing. There is clean, healthy internal competition and we are keeping the money in Canada. What is the result? To-day you can buy better rubbers made in Canada as cheaply as in the United States. Furthermore, we export more rubber goods per head of population than any country on earth, and that condition in the rubber industry is due to the fact that that industry has had sane, continuous protection.
I contend that if you are going to have protection you must have a tariff that protects; a wish-washy halfway measure, half protection and half free trade, does not amount to anything. To-day, if someone suggested raising the tariff on rubber to 50, 75 or 100 per cent, there would be a terrible howl in this house. But what difference would it make to the price of rubber? Not a cent. If you took the duty right off it would not make the difference of a cent, but that 35 per cent protection is a safeguard. It is no longer protection but a safeguard; that is all. Had all our other industries received that protection they would be in the same position, so that the protection they receive would be no longer protection but a safeguard.
I will not detain the house longer. I simply want to state and state most emphatically that the eastern dairy farmer in Canada cannot be in favour of this resolution. If butter, cheese, eggs and the products of the farm come under a reciprocal arrangement, so far as trade with the United States is concerned, it will be disastrous to us, and for that reason I shall have to vote against the resolution.

There has been no

Those words are contained, I believe, in the speech delivered by Sir John A. Macdonald when he introduced the national policy in 1887. While the Conservative party believes in tariffs in order to protect the workingmen of this country from the competition of cheaper labour in other countries, at the same time we believe that reciprocal trade between

Trade with United States
ourselves and other countries under carefully prepared treaties will benefit all concerned. It is true that our trade with other countries has been restricted and that we need markets for our natural products. It is true that we need markets for cattle, for wheat and for the other products of the farm, but we have needed them for the last ten years. Can hon. gentlemen opposite name one single treaty which they negotiated during the ten years they were in office which sold one dollar's worth of farm products? We had a treaty with Australia, which was later extended to New Zealand, which sold manufactured goods, but the farmers of Canada paid for that sale by the opening of the Canadian market to butter, while my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) declared that wheat products could find their own market, and that the Department of Trade and Commerce was not so much interested in the sale of these commodities as in the sale of manufactured goods. As soon as hon. gentlemen opposite got into opposition they became great friends of the people who want to sell natural products. When we came into office we proceeded to make the Canadian market available to Canadian farmers.

speechtext:
If my hon. friend knew what the prices were she would realize that the prices of farm products in Canada are better than in any other part of the world, and that is due in great part to the action taken by this government. After having given the farmers of this country the Canadian market, which they never had under the government of hon. gentlemen opposite, we turned to the problem of finding a market abroad. Whatever else may be -said of them, the treaties into which we have entered were framed with the intent of selling the products of the farm, of the forest, of the mine and of the sea. In return we have agreed to facilitate the importation of manufactured goods from the mother country. While we were trying to find this market within the empire for our farm products, hon. gentlemen opposite were fighting us tooth and nail. Why are they so anxious to trade with the United States, with Russia or with any other country while they fight so bitterly against trading with the mother country? As a result of the treaties we made we are selling farm products in that market.
Let me point out that the United Kingdom market is likely to be open to us so long as we are able to supply it. If we make a treaty with the United States have we any guarantee that the treaty will be continued?
Hon. gentlemen opposite say we should not make a treaty that will be continuous at all; they want us to make one that can be abrogated the next day. They do not believe in five year terms. Are we to give up the British market once more in order to get the United States market, which we may have for fifteen minutes, for five years or for as long as they choose to allow us to enter? Over and over again we have extended our trade east and west; then we began to trade with the United States until our east and west channels were closed up; then the United States market was closed to us, as happened in 1866, and we had no markets at all. Nothing in the imperial conference treaties precludes us from negotiating treaties with other countries, so long as subsequent treaties are negotiated in accordance with the terms of the treaties already made.
Hon. gentlemen opposite suggest that we should approach the United States in the hope of getting reciprocity. Why? We are told that the opportunity exists now because President Roosevelt is said to be in favour of lower tariffs. Let me remind hon. gentlemen what happened to President Wilson when he attempted to reduce the United States tariff a few years ago. At the next election his party was swept out of office. My hon. friends say that the reason they did not do this in the ten years during which they were in office was that a favourable opportunity had not presented itself, and now they say that a favourable opportunity does exist. What is the favourable opportunity? Not a single thing has been said on the other side of the house to indicate that the American government is any more favourable to taking Canadian farm products into that country than they were before. More than that, President-elect Roosevelt in the course of his election campaign declared that he did not know of one single item in the farm schedules on which the duty was too high. He was prepared to lower duties where they were too high, but he did not know of one single item where they were too high. Does that offer us any opportunity to sell our natural products?
It is very necessary that the quality of Canadian goods going to Great Britain should not be impaired. I remember hearing years ago Mr. Andrew Broder, the old member for Dundas, long since dead, telling what had happened to Canadian products when we had reciprocity with the United States. Canadian butter of good quality was sent across the lino into the United States. It was stamped as American butter and sold in the British
Trade aith United States

market as such, while cheap American butter was stamped as Canadian butter and shipped from New York to the British market as a Canadian product. The result was that it took us a long time to regain the reputation for Canadian products in the British market which we had lost in those years.
If there is any possibility of opening up trade negotiations with the United States, if there is any disposition on the part of the United States to reduce their tariffs as they affect Canada and to do business with us, that feeling in the United States is not due to the attitude my hon. friends took in the spring of 1930 when they declared that they were afraid to increase their general tariff and were afraid to increase the British preference lest it might provoke the United States and be misunderstood on the other side of the line. If any favourable attitude has arisen in the United States in recent years it is due to the fact that this country has taken an independent, manly stand with .respect to its own economic affairs. It is due to the fact that this government has put into force tariff schedules calculated to meet the interests of the people of this country, regardless of whether they provoke the United States or any other country. And if to-day the United States are prepared to deal with us, it is because they respect the attitude we have taken and realize that they are dealing with people whom they can neither browbeat nor frighten, people who are not afraid, people who will do what is best in their own interests, regardless of whether anybody in the United States disapproves or not.
To-day the Hearst press, which helped to elect President Roosevelt, is printing its diatribes against any reductions in their tariff. They are urging still higher tariffs so as to make up for the depreciation in currency in those countries which are trying to trade with them. It is true that this country needs trade. The people need internal trade even more than they do external. It is the fact that we had an external trade that makes us so susceptible during this time of depression.
